SECTION I
I.	Activists and lawyers in Africa are calling for urgent action to protect women, girls and boys as
digital violence surges across the continent. A massive rise in internet users, coupled with
huge numbers of people aged under 30, has fuelled an increase in gendered online violence
across the continent, according to experts, by giving perpetrators new tools to control and
silence women and girls, and influence boys. Unfortunately, the world offline is not safe, equal
and inclusive. But the world online is proliferating that to such an extent that it’s creating a
foundation for a very, very unequal future.
In Africa, internet access is growing exponentially and more than 70% of the population of sub-
Saharan Africa is under 30. We know that young people generally face higher rates of online
violence and very often are bigger users of any tech. Digital violence against women and girls
has devastating effects such as mental health problems, withdrawal from public and economic
life, physical attacks on LGBTQI+ people in countries that criminalise homosexuality, and
femicide. While there is very little pan-African research, one study across five countries in sub-
Saharan Africa showed that 28% of women had experienced online violence. As internet access
expands, this number is expected to rise. Only 38% of people on the continent are internet
users, according to the International Telecommunication Union — and among women the figure
falls to 31%. Studies, research and anecdotal evidence at a national level paint a horrifying
picture of extreme levels of violence and a toxic online environment with dire real-life
consequences.
Extensive research conducted in Ethiopia over the past four years by the Centre for
Information Resilience (CIR) found that gendered abuse is so endemic online it has become
normalised. One Ethiopian woman interviewed by CIR said “no platform feels safe”. The
researchers found that while men are attacked online for ideas and opinions, women receive
misogynistic abuse related to their appearance and role in society. Threats and intimidation
also migrate offline, putting women at risk of physical attack.
Globally, nearly two in every five women will experience tech-facilitated violence while 85% of
women who are online have witnessed or encountered online abuse. Fewer than 40% of
countries have laws protecting women from cyber harassment or cyber stalking, leaving 44% of
the world’s women and girls — 1.8 billion — without access to legal protection. [Sociology; Word
Count: 389]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://www.theguardian.com/global-
development /2026/mar/30/urgent-action-needed-to-prevent-surge-in-digital-violence-in-
africa-experts-say
content.questionText: Which inference most reasonably follows from the author’s argument?
options: Digital access mainly repeats older harms without worsening them.
Online growth is expanding faster than the violence it enables.
Digital expansion may deepen inequality when protections remain absent.
Internet access chiefly empowers vulnerable groups against offline bias.
content.explanation: This option is the strongest inference because it captures the author’s underlying causal logic: when existing social inequality enters rapidly expanding digital systems without safeguards, it becomes more entrenched and more scalable. The passage moves beyond description and warns that technological growth, without protection, can structurally intensify injustice.

I.	Activists and lawyers in Africa are calling for urgent action to protect women, girls and boys as
digital violence surges across the continent. A massive rise in internet users, coupled with
huge numbers of people aged under 30, has fuelled an increase in gendered online violence
across the continent, according to experts, by giving perpetrators new tools to control and
silence women and girls, and influence boys. Unfortunately, the world offline is not safe, equal
and inclusive. But the world online is proliferating that to such an extent that it’s creating a
foundation for a very, very unequal future.
In Africa, internet access is growing exponentially and more than 70% of the population of sub-
Saharan Africa is under 30. We know that young people generally face higher rates of online
violence and very often are bigger users of any tech. Digital violence against women and girls
has devastating effects such as mental health problems, withdrawal from public and economic
life, physical attacks on LGBTQI+ people in countries that criminalise homosexuality, and
femicide. While there is very little pan-African research, one study across five countries in sub-
Saharan Africa showed that 28% of women had experienced online violence. As internet access
expands, this number is expected to rise. Only 38% of people on the continent are internet
users, according to the International Telecommunication Union — and among women the figure
falls to 31%. Studies, research and anecdotal evidence at a national level paint a horrifying
picture of extreme levels of violence and a toxic online environment with dire real-life
consequences.
Extensive research conducted in Ethiopia over the past four years by the Centre for
Information Resilience (CIR) found that gendered abuse is so endemic online it has become
normalised. One Ethiopian woman interviewed by CIR said “no platform feels safe”. The
researchers found that while men are attacked online for ideas and opinions, women receive
misogynistic abuse related to their appearance and role in society. Threats and intimidation
also migrate offline, putting women at risk of physical attack.
Globally, nearly two in every five women will experience tech-facilitated violence while 85% of
women who are online have witnessed or encountered online abuse. Fewer than 40% of
countries have laws protecting women from cyber harassment or cyber stalking, leaving 44% of
the world’s women and girls — 1.8 billion — without access to legal protection. [Sociology; Word
Count: 389]

II.	It is impossible to capture seven decades of formidable intellect, wrapped into some 14,000
books and articles, in less than a thousand words. Yet German philosopher Jiirgen Habermas
staked his career on the power of dialogue and deliberation, so it is worth chiming in.
Habermas, who died on March 14 at the age of 96, was among the greatest thinkers of our
time. He was unshakeable in his conviction that people have minds of their own, can hope for a
better future, and have the capability, collectively and democratically, to bring that future to
life. Born in Diisseldorf in 1929, he escaped conscription to the Wehrmacht by a whisker. His
later realisation that, as a child, he had been enveloped by “a politically criminal system of

Nazism” propelled him into a lifelong scholarly, political and personal campaign to rescue
democracy and restore the future. It was an uphill struggle of breathtaking proportions. If the
best was still to come, the journey towards enlightenment would require “nothing less than a
comprehensive theory of modern society and its underlying dynamics”.
That was the scholarly project, and few 20th century theorists could tackle it. Habermas led
the way with sweeping interdisciplinary reach: historical understanding, geographical
imagination, sociological insight, grasp of legal theory, sustained engagement with ethics,
aesthetics, psychology, epistemology, theology and more. Any one of these approaches would
have moved the dial, but in Habermas they came together with a powerful political message.
Variously described as a socialist, democrat, internationalist, and above all humanitarian, his
philosophy — practical, perhaps pragmatic — was his politics. Its centrepiece was the formation,
functioning and fragility of a public sphere — Offentlichkeit — mediating between states and
civil societies, promising an alternative to the authoritarian, totalitarian regimes he eschewed.
Bookended by two landmark works, Habermas’s lifelong conviction was that the formation of
public opinion through rational, reasoned conversation was vital for the conduct and survival
of parliamentary democracy. Both works are cautionary tales concerned equally with the forces
stifling deliberative democracy and with the conditions in which it might flourish.
[Philosophy; Word Count: 337]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://theconversation.com/jurgen-

Il.	If Bazball is dead — and obituaries are being written furiously — it would be a pity. England
didn’t invent the attacking, free-flowing style, nor are they the first team to display a passion
for the game that seems to go beyond victory and defeat. The great West Indies teams of the
past played cricket with similar enthusiasm, each player expressing himself. However, Bazball
seems un-English in the land of Geoff Boycott and Alastair Cook, defensive batters of great
skill but all too aware that cricket was a livelihood and caution mattered above all.
Skipper Ben Stokes and coach Brendon ‘Baz’ McCullum see cricket as entertainment, feel they
owe something to the spectators, thoughts that would not have occurred to earlier generations.
It probably helped that they were both born in New Zealand, the land of bungee-jumping and
zorbing where it is difficult to take sports too seriously. According to Michael Brearley,
England’s high priest as successful captaincy and psychoanalyst, Bazball was born out of
depression. Stokes came through a court case (for affray), the death of his father and injury,
while McCullum, who had lost interest in the game at one time, was keen on players
rediscovering the simple joys of playing it. An awareness that asked, like Eliot, “Where is the
life we have lost in living?”
In Bazball, players “ran towards the danger”; failure didn’t mean excommunication. It has
succeeded in its three and a half years now despite the scepticism of those who believed it was
all a con. Opponents couldn’t put a finger on what Bazball was, and sometimes neither could
England. But it worked brilliantly, with England winning Tests with fabulous fourth-innings
chases against Pakistan, New Zealand and India. The sight of Joe Root reverse scooping fast

bowlers for six seemed to give Bazball the final stamp of approval from one of the greats who
swore by established technique.
Perhaps Bazball is best enjoyed by those who have no skin in the game. It is glorious cricket
for those outside England who are not so invested in the result. Would an Indian batter be
forgiven for getting out repeatedly because he kept making the same mistake, although on
other occasions the identical shot fetched tons of runs and encomiums?
To enjoy, even encourage an approach when it works but call it ‘stupid’ when it fails is bad
faith.
[Sports; Word Count: 392]

make-despite-losses/article70376198.ece

Il.	If Bazball is dead — and obituaries are being written furiously — it would be a pity. England
didn’t invent the attacking, free-flowing style, nor are they the first team to display a passion
for the game that seems to go beyond victory and defeat. The great West Indies teams of the
past played cricket with similar enthusiasm, each player expressing himself. However, Bazball
seems un-English in the land of Geoff Boycott and Alastair Cook, defensive batters of great
skill but all too aware that cricket was a livelihood and caution mattered above all.
Skipper Ben Stokes and coach Brendon ‘Baz’ McCullum see cricket as entertainment, feel they
owe something to the spectators, thoughts that would not have occurred to earlier generations.
It probably helped that they were both born in New Zealand, the land of bungee-jumping and
zorbing where it is difficult to take sports too seriously. According to Michael Brearley,
England’s high priest as successful captaincy and psychoanalyst, Bazball was born out of
depression. Stokes came through a court case (for affray), the death of his father and injury,
while McCullum, who had lost interest in the game at one time, was keen on players
rediscovering the simple joys of playing it. An awareness that asked, like Eliot, “Where is the
life we have lost in living?”
In Bazball, players “ran towards the danger”; failure didn’t mean excommunication. It has
succeeded in its three and a half years now despite the scepticism of those who believed it was
all a con. Opponents couldn’t put a finger on what Bazball was, and sometimes neither could
England. But it worked brilliantly, with England winning Tests with fabulous fourth-innings
chases against Pakistan, New Zealand and India. The sight of Joe Root reverse scooping fast

bowlers for six seemed to give Bazball the final stamp of approval from one of the greats who
swore by established technique.
Perhaps Bazball is best enjoyed by those who have no skin in the game. It is glorious cricket
for those outside England who are not so invested in the result. Would an Indian batter be
forgiven for getting out repeatedly because he kept making the same mistake, although on
other occasions the identical shot fetched tons of runs and encomiums?
To enjoy, even encourage an approach when it works but call it ‘stupid’ when it fails is bad
faith.

IV.	According to media theorist Marshall McLuhan, every medium is an extension of our physical
or mental faculties. The hammer extends our fist, the spear our teeth, the hut our skin, the
wheel our feet — and electronic media extend our central nervous system to all of humankind.
Extended abilities give us new powers but disrupt previous sensory, cognitive, and social
settings. As humankind switched to the internet, printing no longer defines the protocols
humans live by. Print-based culture is collapsing. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The era of printing was, in fact, very short by historical standards — about 550 years. Some
call this period the Gutenberg Parenthesis — a metaphor popularized by Jeff Jarvis. Within
this Parenthesis, communication was centered around fixed, authored, linear, and stable texts.
Things were different before books. Communication was fluid and situational, passed mostly
through direct interaction between people. The internet has largely restored those conditions:
digital content is updated, shared, and much of it is user-generated — just like in orality.
Books withdrew both author and reader from the surrounding reality and turned them inward,
into contemplation. Before literacy, it was different — people were immersed in the flow of
events. This pattern returns: people are once again immersed in a flow — this time, a digital
one.
As digital media reverse the cognitive detachment typical of print culture and retrieve the
situational immersion typical of orality, not only is the Gutenberg Parenthesis closing, but the
metaphor of a closing parenthesis — or arc — can be extended to the entire era of literacy. The
environmental detachment as a media effect appeared before print — it was the effect of
writing. Writing separated the known from the knower (Havelock) and made it possible to
contemplate things “from outside” interaction with them.
“Oral Greek did not know what an object of thought was,” wrote Havelock. To catch thought,
the flow of words had to be arrested, and words needed to be captured and separated from the
thinker. Writing made this possible by putting words before the individual for contemplation.
Intellectual and spiritual awakening pulled humans out of the natural cycles of thoughtless

survival and led them to inquire into the meaning of life, the universe, and everything. The
Axial Age began transforming humans’ tribal existence into complex societies.
[Humanities; Word Count: 370]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://bigthink.com/the-present/the-digital-
ages-reversion-to-pre-literate-communication/

situational immersion typical of orality, not only is the Gutenberg Parenthesis closing, but the

thinker. Writing made this possible by putting words before the individual for contemplation.

survival and led them to inquire into the meaning of life, the universe, and everything. The

VII. Delimitation is the process of redrawing the boundaries of electoral constituencies to ensure
equal representation for equal populations. It is carried out to reflect changes in population as
recorded in the census, so that each constituency has, as far as possible, an equal number of
inhabitants. In India, delimitation is conducted by the Delimitation Commission of India, an
independent body whose decisions have the force of law and cannot ordinarily be challenged in
court. This process helps maintain fairness in the democratic system by ensuring that
representation in legislative bodies remains proportionate to population changes.
In India, delimitation is carried out based on the provisions of the Constitution of India and
the Delimitation Commission Acts enacted by Parliament. The number of seats allocated to
each state in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies is determined on the basis of
population figures from the census. However, to encourage population control measures, the
readjustment of seats has been frozen until after the first census conducted post-2026.
Delimitation plays a crucial role in strengthening representative democracy by ensuring
balanced political representation and equitable distribution of constituencies across the
country.

one of the largest annual religious gatherings in the world.

XII. The 42nd Amendment of the Constitution of India, enacted in 1976 during the Emergency, is
one of the most far-reaching constitutional amendments in Indian history and is often
described as the “Mini-Constitution.” Its background lies in the political turbulence of the
1970s, particularly after the Golaknath case (1967), which intensified conflict between the
judiciary and the executive over Parliament’s amending power. The Allahabad High Court
judgment against Prime Minister Indira Gandhi for election malpractice further deepened the
crisis. After the declaration of Emergency on 25 June 1975, the government acquired
extraordinary powers and introduced several constitutional changes, of which the 42nd
Amendment was the most comprehensive. Its objectives were to strengthen executive power,
curtail judicial review, enhance Parliament’s authority, centralise administration, and reshape
the Constitution in line with the government’s political and ideological agenda.
The amendment introduced sweeping changes across the Constitution. In the Preamble, it
added the words “Socialist” and “Secular” and changed “unity of the nation” to “unity and

integrity of the nation.” It expanded the Directive Principles of State Policy by inserting
Articles 39A, 43A, and 48A, dealing with free legal aid, workers’ participation in management,
and environmental protection, and amended Article 39(f) for child welfare. It also inserted Part
IV-A, introducing Fundamental Duties of citizens. In the Seventh Schedule, subjects such as
education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and
administration of justice were shifted from the State List to the Concurrent List, increasing
central control. It formalised the rule that the President must act on the advice of the Cabinet,
inserted Article 257A to allow deployment of central forces in states, abolished quorum
requirements in legislatures, and extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies
from five years to six years. The amendment also altered emergency provisions, allowed
national emergency to apply to the whole or part of India, extended the duration of President’s
Rule, restricted High Courts’ jurisdiction, required a seven-judge bench with a two-thirds
majority in certain constitutional cases, inserted Part XIV-A with Articles 323A and 323B for
tribunals, and expanded the operation of Article 358 for suspension of Article 19 rights during
emergencies.
The amendment faced strong criticism for weakening democracy, federalism, and judicial
independence. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down
important parts of the amendment, especially provisions that gave Parliament unlimited
amending power and curtailed judicial review, and reaffirmed the Basic Structure Doctrine.
After the Emergency, the 43rd and 44th Amendments reversed many of its excesses. Thus, the
42nd Amendment remains a landmark example of both constitutional overreach and the
resilience of judicial review in India.www.lawpreptutorial.com

indian-constitution/

It removed “Sovereign” and “Democratic” and inserted “Federal” and “Presidential”,

and integrity of the nation” in Preamble.

It deleted the Preamble entirely, shifting all ideals into Directive Principles, arguing
judges often misused the opening words to block reforms earlier.

described as the “Mini-Constitution.” Its background lies in the political turbulence of the
1970s, particularly after the Golaknath case (1967), which intensified conflict between the
judiciary and the executive over Parliament’s amending power. The Allahabad High Court
judgment against Prime Minister Indira Gandhi for election malpractice further deepened the
crisis. After the declaration of Emergency on 25 June 1975, the government acquired
extraordinary powers and introduced several constitutional changes, of which the 42nd
Amendment was the most comprehensive. Its objectives were to strengthen executive power,
curtail judicial review, enhance Parliament’s authority, centralise administration, and reshape
the Constitution in line with the government’s political and ideological agenda.
The amendment introduced sweeping changes across the Constitution. In the Preamble, it
added the words “Socialist” and “Secular” and changed “unity of the nation” to “unity and

integrity of the nation.” It expanded the Directive Principles of State Policy by inserting
Articles 39A, 43A, and 48A, dealing with free legal aid, workers’ participation in management,
and environmental protection, and amended Article 39(f) for child welfare. It also inserted Part
IV-A, introducing Fundamental Duties of citizens. In the Seventh Schedule, subjects such as
education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and
administration of justice were shifted from the State List to the Concurrent List, increasing
central control. It formalised the rule that the President must act on the advice of the Cabinet,
inserted Article 257A to allow deployment of central forces in states, abolished quorum
requirements in legislatures, and extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies
from five years to six years. The amendment also altered emergency provisions, allowed
national emergency to apply to the whole or part of India, extended the duration of President’s
Rule, restricted High Courts’ jurisdiction, required a seven-judge bench with a two-thirds
majority in certain constitutional cases, inserted Part XIV-A with Articles 323A and 323B for
tribunals, and expanded the operation of Article 358 for suspension of Article 19 rights during
emergencies.
The amendment faced strong criticism for weakening democracy, federalism, and judicial
independence. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down
important parts of the amendment, especially provisions that gave Parliament unlimited
amending power and curtailed judicial review, and reaffirmed the Basic Structure Doctrine.
After the Emergency, the 43rd and 44th Amendments reversed many of its excesses. Thus, the
42nd Amendment remains a landmark example of both constitutional overreach and the
resilience of judicial review in India.www.lawpreptutorial.com

indian-constitution/

It reduced Lok Sabha term to four years, restored quorum rules, and barred central forces

Parliament supreme by removing meaningful judicial review over constitutional changes. Her

structural limitation doctrine. The student is asked to name the decision and the holding that
answers this debate.
Which option most directly matches that judicial response?

Golaknath (1967) struck down the amendment entirely, restored judicial review, and
declared Parliament has no power to amend any provision at all.

Kesavananda Bharati (1973) approved unlimited amending power, removed basic structure
limits, and barred courts from reviewing constitutional amendments thereafter
permanently in India.

Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975) upheld the amendment, validated curbs on judicial review,
and extended legislative terms, holding elections need not be fair.

Minerva Mills (1980) struck down important parts giving Parliament unlimited amending
power and curtailing judicial review, reaffirming the Basic Structure Doctrine again.

XII. Mens rea means the guilty mental state that ordinarily accompanies a criminal act. This
article explains it through the maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea: an act does not
make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty. It notes that mens rea was not always
treated as an ingredient of crime; in earlier periods, punishment could follow even without
proof of intention. Over time, especially from the seventeenth century onward, criminal law
came to recognise that blameworthy conduct usually requires both a wrongful act and a
blameworthy state of mind. In India, this idea entered criminal law through English influence
and became reflected across the Indian Penal Code, even though the phrase “mens rea” itself is
not expressly used in the Code. The article points out that many IPC offences use words such
as “voluntarily,” “dishonestly,” “knowingly,” and “fraudulently,” which embody the idea of a
guilty mind.
The passage identifies four main forms of mens rea: intention, knowledge, recklessness, and
negligence. Intention refers to a deliberate mental decision to bring about a consequence;
knowledge refers to awareness of facts and likely consequences; recklessness means foreseeing
a risk but proceeding with indifference to it; and negligence is failure to exercise the degree of
care that a prudent person would have used in the circumstances. It also emphasises that
mens rea is usually essential in criminal law unless a statute expressly or by necessary
implication excludes it. The Supreme Court decisions discussed, such as Ravule Hariprasada
Rao v. State and State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George, support the principle that guilty
mind is generally presumed to be a component of criminal liability unless legislation clearly
rules it out.
Another key point in the article is the need for concurrence of mens rea and actus reus: the
guilty mind and the wrongful act must exist together for criminal liability in the ordinary case.

Mere intention without the act, or the act without the corresponding guilty state of mind, will
not usually be enough. At the same time, it notes important exceptions, especially strict
liability offences, where proof of mens rea is not required. Examples listed include criminal
libel, public nuisance, contempt of court, kidnapping/abduction, bigamy, rape, sale of obscene
books, and certain statutory offences under laws such as the Essential Commodities Act and
the Motor Vehicles Act. The overall conclusion of the article is that mens rea remains a
foundational idea in criminal law, but its role depends on the language, structure, and purpose
of the particular offence.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://blog.ipleaders.in/all-you-need-to-
know-about-mens-rea/

Kunal angrily writes in his diary that he intends to burn his neighbour’s shed “next weekend.”
Two days later, while Kunal is out of town, a short circuit in the neighbour’s shed causes a fire
and the shed burns down. Police find Kunal’s diary during a separate inquiry and arrest him
for the burning, claiming his written intention proves guilt. Kunal argues he never performed
any act leading to the fire and was not even present.
How should liability be assessed on these facts?
options:
Kunal is liable because intention alone proves guilt, and the diary entry substitutes for the
act when harm eventually occurs later.

Kunal is liable because presence is irrelevant, and any earlier intention attaches to later
events, even if caused independently by accident.

Kunal is not liable because the guilty mind and the wrongful act must exist together, and
here the act occurred without his mind.

Kunal is not liable because diaries are privileged, so courts cannot ever use them, even if
they show intent to commit crime.

Therefore, the ordinary basis for criminal liability is not satisfied.

A delivery driver, Neel, sees a bright warning sign that a bridge ahead is under repair and
may collapse under heavy vehicles. He thinks, “It will probably be fine,” and drives his loaded
truck across anyway to save time. The bridge collapses, causing injury. Neel claims he did not
desire the collapse and therefore lacked intention. The prosecution argues that he foresaw a
risk and proceeded with indifference to it.
Which mental state most closely fits his conduct as described?
options:
Intention, because he deliberately drove, so he must be treated as wanting the collapse
outcome, regardless of what he believed.

Knowledge, because he was fully certain collapse would occur, and acted with awareness
that the consequence would happen inevitably anyway.

Recklessness, because he foresaw a risk but proceeded with indifference to it, treating the
warning as ignorable for convenience.

Negligence, because he had no awareness at all, and only failed to take care due to
momentary forgetfulness, not risk-taking.
content.explanation: The option directly uses the passage’s category “recklessness” and mirrors the described definition: “foreseeing a risk but proceeding with indifference.” Neel saw a warning, appreciated danger, and still drove to save time, which fits recklessness more than intention, knowledge, or mere negligence.

A newspaper editor publishes a harsh, false article accusing a citizen of corruption, believing the
allegation to be true because a source told him so. The citizen sues and also seeks criminal action,
and the editor argues he lacked any guilty mind because he honestly believed the claim and had no
intention to harm. The complainant replies that certain offences do not require proof of mens rea
and are treated as strict liability in law.
Which statement best reflects the passage’s point about exceptions?
options:
The editor must be acquitted because mens rea is always essential, and honest belief
automatically defeats every criminal offence in all cases.

The editor may still face liability because strict liability offences exist where proof of mens rea
is not required, as it is an exception.

The editor must be acquitted because strict liability applies only to traffic violations, and never
to publication-related offences in criminal law.

The editor must be acquitted because civil suits are the only remedy for publications, and
criminal law never recognises any publication offence.

believing it is her own. Thirty minutes later, she opens it in a taxi, realises it belongs to someone

complaint alleging theft because Asha physically carried the bag away. Asha argues she never had

How should liability be approached?

Liable because taking another’s property is theft per se and later return cannot erase the
offence once it is complete.

Liable because negligence is enough for dishonest taking, and confusion about bags still shows
a careless intent to deprive.

Not liable because punishment follows even without intention, and earlier periods allowed guilt
without proof of mind.

Not liable because mens rea means a guilty mental state accompanying a criminal act, and her
belief lacked guilt.

breach of notification shall be punished,” without mentioning “knowingly” or “intentionally.” Riya, a

did not know it contained prohibited goods. The prosecution argues that because the statute is
silent on intention, guilt is automatic and knowledge is irrelevant. Riya argues guilty mind is
normally presumed unless the law clearly rules it out.
Which position best matches the passage principle?

Defence barred: statutory silence always excludes mens rea; liability becomes automatic for
every offence, so knowledge is irrelevant.

Defence considered: guilty mind is generally presumed unless legislation clearly rules it out,
though words like knowingly are absent here.

Defence barred: strict liability covers all import offences; courts never examine intent or
knowledge, so her explanation cannot matter.

Defence must succeed: mens rea is always essential; no offence exists without explicit intention
wording, so the prosecution fails automatically.

XIV. The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to
guardian and ward. Before this legislation, guardianship matters were governed by different
personal laws and judicial practices. The Act introduced a uniform procedural framework with
the objective of providing a judicial mechanism for appointment and declaration of guardians,
protecting the person and property of minors, regulating the powers, duties, and liabilities of
guardians, preventing misuse of a minor’s property, and ensuring that the welfare of the minor
remains the controlling consideration. The Act extends to the whole of India and applies to all
minors under the Indian Majority Act, 1875, that is, ordinarily persons below 18 years, and
covers guardians of the person, property, or both. It becomes relevant in situations such as
death of parents, custody disputes, divorce or separation, management of minor’s property,
appointment of a guardian, or removal of an existing guardian. Though it does not override
specific adoption laws, guardianship disputes may still come within its scope.
Section 4 defines the key expressions: a minor is a person who has not attained majority, a
guardian is a person having care of the person or property of a minor or both, a ward is a
minor for whom there is a guardian, and the Court generally means the District Court having
jurisdiction. The Act is divided into four chapters dealing with preliminary matters,
appointment and declaration of guardians, duties and liabilities of guardians, and
supplemental provisions. Under Section 7, the Court may appoint or declare a guardian where
necessary for the welfare of the minor. Under Section 8, applications may be made by a
proposed guardian, a relative or friend, the Collector, or any authorised person. Section 9
governs jurisdiction, Section 10 prescribes the contents of the application, and Section 12
empowers the Court to issue interim orders for production, custody, or protection of property.
The most important provision is Section 17, which makes the welfare of the minor the guiding
principle and requires the Court to consider factors such as age, sex, religion, character and
capacity of the proposed guardian, nearness of kin, wishes of a deceased parent, and even the

intelligent preference of the minor if old enough. Section 19 places restrictions on appointment
where fit natural guardians are living.
Chapter III regulates the duties, rights, and liabilities of guardians. Under Section 20, the
guardian stands in a fiduciary position toward the ward. Sections 24 to 26 deal with the
guardian of the person, who is responsible for custody, support, health, education, and cannot
remove the minor from jurisdiction without permission. Sections 27, 29, and 31 deal with
guardians of property, requiring ordinary prudence in management and court permission
before sale, mortgage, transfer, or long lease of immovable property.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lawcrust.in/guardians-and-wards-
act-1890/

How should the court approach the decision?

priority depends on filing time.

A 14-year-old ward, Arman, owns a small apartment inherited from his mother. His current
guardian, a distant cousin, begins negotiating a quick sale and tells neighbours he will “finalise it
this week.” Arman’s school principal learns this and informs the court that Arman is being
pressured to sign papers. A relative files an urgent request asking the court to immediately stop
any sale and to secure the property documents until a full guardianship inquiry is completed. The
guardian argues nothing can be done until final appointment proceedings end.
What can the court do at this stage?
options:
Court may issue interim orders for custody or protection of property so documents and
possession can be secured immediately to prevent misuse.

The court cannot pass any interim order because guardianship disputes require a full trial first,
and urgent directions are barred by law.

Court may only punish the guardian criminally, because civil courts cannot interfere with
property negotiations unless fraud is already proved fully.

The court must allow the sale because guardians have absolute property powers, and minors’
property can be disposed of without court supervision.

Rina is appointed guardian of her nephew Dev (a minor) and is given control over Dev’s rental
income. Rina starts depositing the rent into her personal account and uses it to fund her own
business expansion, promising that she will “repay later with profit.” Dev’s grandmother challenges
this conduct and seeks the court’s intervention, arguing that a guardian must not treat the ward’s
money as personal capital. Rina argues she is “family” and acted in Dev’s best interest by investing.
What is the best legal view?
options:
Guardian stands in a fiduciary position toward the ward, so personal use of the ward’s funds
breaches the duty even if repayment is promised.

Guardian is like an owner of the ward’s income, so using it for personal business is allowed as
long as some benefit is intended.

Guardian owes only moral duties, not legal ones, so court cannot intervene unless the guardian
admits dishonesty in writing first.

A guardian may freely invest the ward’s money in any venture without constraints, because
family relationships remove fiduciary duties altogether.
content.explanation: The option directly uses “fiduciary position toward the ward,” matching the reference line. A fiduciary cannot mix the ward’s assets with personal business interests or treat the ward’s money as private capital, because fiduciary duty demands loyalty and avoidance of conflict.

“appointment” is needed because both are natural parents. The court is asked to intervene
formally to settle authority and reduce conflict.
Under what condition can the court appoint or declare a guardian in such a situation?

The court may appoint a guardian only when relatives consent unanimously, because
courts cannot interfere in parental disputes without family agreement.

The court may appoint a guardian only if both parents die, because living parents always
bar the court from making any declaration.

The court may appoint a guardian only if the minor owns property, because guardianship
of the person is private and courts cannot decide it.

Court may appoint or declare a guardian where necessary for the welfare of the minor,
even if parents dispute custody and control.

validates any guardian sale of land on behalf of minors.

Permission is required only for movable property, because immovable property is stable

No permission required if guardian believes it benefits ward, because subjective belief
overrides procedural safeguards for property transfers entirely.

content.passageText:
XV. Malicious prosecution under the law of tort means the wrongful institution of legal
proceedings, usually criminal, against a person without reasonable and probable cause and
with a malicious intention. The iPleaders article explains that Black’s Law Dictionary defines
it as a legal proceeding initiated without probable cause and with harmful intent, and the
Supreme Court in West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray (2006) described it
as misuse of the legal system to harm another person without valid justification. The article
also distinguishes malicious prosecution from abuse of process and abuse of power. Malicious
prosecution concerns the wrongful starting of proceedings at the very beginning, whereas
abuse of process refers to misuse of a legal process after it has been properly initiated, and
abuse of power concerns misuse of official authority outside the courtroom context.

The article identifies five essential elements that a plaintiff must prove in an action for
malicious prosecution: prosecution by the defendant, absence of reasonable and probable cause,
malice, termination of proceedings in favour of the plaintiff, and damage suffered by the
plaintiff. “Prosecution” is used in a wider sense than a trial and can include criminal
proceedings by way of appeal or revision, though the article notes that mere proceedings before
a police officer have been held not to amount to prosecution, while the position regarding
quasi-judicial authorities has been treated differently in different cases. Absence of reasonable
and probable cause means the prosecution had no justified basis. Malice does not necessarily
mean personal spite; it may also mean any improper purpose, such as gaining a collateral
advantage. Proceedings must have terminated in favour of the plaintiff, which generally
means there is no judicial determination of guilt, and the plaintiff must show actual damage,
which the article groups into damage to reputation, person, or property. The burden of proving
all these essentials lies on the plaintiff.
The article further notes that earlier courts were reluctant to recognise malicious civil
proceedings, but later decisions accepted that malicious abuse of civil proceedings may also be
actionable if bad intention, absence of reasonable cause, favourable termination, and resulting
harm are proved. As for remedies, the article says that the aggrieved person may file a suit for
damages, including compensation for injury to reputation and recovery of legal costs, and in
appropriate cases may also seek constitutional relief under Articles 32 or 226. The principal
defences available to a defendant are the presence of reasonable grounds and proof of good
faith, that is, showing that the proceedings were started honestly and not to misuse the legal
system.

Ramesh runs a street-food cart and publicly criticises the local licensing officer on social media.
The officer, without filing any case or approaching any court, cancels Ramesh’s vending licence
the next morning and orders municipal staff to seize his cart, saying it is “punishment for
disrespect.” Ramesh later learns that no notice or hearing was given and no proceedings were
initiated. He considers a tort action and must identify whether the wrong is about starting
proceedings, misusing process later, or misusing official authority outside court.
How should this conduct be classified?
options:
It is wrongful institution at the beginning, because a baseless case was instituted without
cause solely to harm the target.

It is misuse of legal process after properly initiated, because court steps were exploited
later to pressure settlement and silence criticism.

It is misuse of official authority outside the courtroom context, because power was used
administratively to punish the person without proceedings.

It is neither, because official decisions and court tactics can never be questioned in tort,
whatever the motive behind them.
content.explanation: The option directly uses “misuse of official authority outside courtroom context,” matching the reference line’s description of abuse of power. Since the officer punished Ramesh through official administrative action without invoking court proceedings, this classification is the best fit.

After a neighbour dispute, Sunil was prosecuted for assault on the basis of a complaint lodged by
Vikram. The criminal case ended in Sunil’s acquittal because witnesses turned hostile and the court
found insufficient evidence to convict. Sunil files a civil suit alleging malicious prosecution and claims
Vikram acted with improper motive and no reasonable basis. Vikram responds that acquittal alone does
not win the tort claim and argues the law places the duty of proving each required element on the person
who sues.
Who carries the burden?
options:
The burden lies on the defendant to prove innocence of motive, because filing a complaint creates a
presumption of malice in civil court.

Burden lies on plaintiff to prove prosecution, absence of cause, malice, favourable termination, and
damage, since all essentials must be shown here.

Burden lies on court to investigate facts suo motu, because tort claims are public law matters and
parties need not prove elements.

Burden lies on plaintiff only to show acquittal, because termination in his favour implies absence of
cause and malice in each case.

Neha worked as an accountant in a small firm. One weekend, cash went missing from the office drawer.
Without checking attendance records or speaking to staff, the owner immediately named Neha in a
criminal complaint; despite knowing she had been out of station and no one saw her near the office.
Police filed charges, but the case was later dropped for want of any supporting material. Neha sues for
malicious prosecution and wants to show there was no reasonable and probable cause.
Which factual situation most directly indicates that absence?
options:
Complainant relied on clear CCTV and a written confession; that supplies a justified basis, even if
court later acquits the accused.

Complainant filed complaint to settle personal scores, yet had verified ledger shortages and witness
statements; motive alone does not erase cause.

The complainant acted after the police advised filing; such advice shows reasonable grounds, so
absence of cause cannot readily be inferred.

The complainant had no witnesses, documents, or facts linking the plaintiff, so the prosecution had
no justified basis for starting proceedings.
content.explanation: This option directly uses the reference idea of “no justified basis” by showing there were no facts linking Neha to the alleged crime. When there are no witnesses, documents, or connecting facts, the prosecution lacks a justified basis to be launched.

Priya must prove negligence in investigation alone, because careless complaints are punishable even
when reasonable grounds exist and there is no malice.

Priya must prove misuse of process after proper filing, since only later procedural abuse, not initial
filing, creates tort liability.

Priya must prove abuse of official authority outside court, because private complainants cannot be
liable for initiating proceedings.

Rohit and a contractor are in a billing dispute about renovation work. To force Rohit to pay
immediately, the contractor files a criminal complaint alleging Rohit stole tools, even though
the contractor’s real aim is to secure a quick settlement and threaten Rohit’s reputation. The
case is later withdrawn after Rohit pays part of the bill, and Rohit sues for malicious
prosecution, arguing the complaint was used for an improper purpose rather than justice.
In assessing malice, what interpretation best matches the passage?
options:
Malice requires personal spite alone, so unless the builder hated the owner personally, the
element fails even if the complaint aimed to pressure payment.

Malice is irrelevant if the case ends in acquittal, because favourable termination
automatically proves improper purpose and replaces the malice requirement.

Malice may mean an improper purpose, such as gaining a collateral advantage, so filing a
complaint to force payment can satisfy the malice requirement.

Malice exists whenever the police investigate, because starting any complaint shows
hostility, and courts presume malicious intention from litigation.

Farida, a teacher, was falsely prosecuted for cheating in an exam on a complaint by a rival
colleague. She was arrested at school, suspended for three months, and local newspapers
reported the allegation. The criminal court later discharged her without any finding of guilt.
Farida files a tort suit and must show actual damage rather than relying on hurt feelings
alone. She claims her reputation suffered, her liberty was restrained, and she spent money on
legal defence.
Which description best captures the kinds of damage recognised for this tort?
options:
Damage may be to reputation, person, or property, so arrest humiliation, medical stress,
and legal fees can satisfy actual damage.

Damage is presumed from acquittal alone, so the plaintiff need not show any injury to
reputation, person, or property.

Only physical injury counts as damage, so reputational harm and litigation costs are
irrelevant to malicious prosecution actions in tort.

Only property loss counts as damage, so arrest and stigma cannot be considered even if
proceedings ended favourably for plaintiff.

It therefore matches the recognised heads of actual damage described in the passage.

SECTION IV
XVI. In the late 20th century, the world came together to plug a hole in the ozone layer — the part
of Earth’s atmosphere that absorbs most of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet radiation. If left
unchecked, this hole would have exposed life on Earth to dangerous — and in some regions
potentially lethal — levels of radiation, but an international treaty brought us back from the
brink of disaster. That treaty, the Montreal Protocol, is a lesson in human resilience: We can
save the world, because we already did it once before.
The story of the Montreal Protocol starts, bizarrely, with an epidemic of deadly fridges in the
1920s. In those pioneer days of electric home refrigeration, everyone’s favorite new kitchen
appliance relied on highly toxic, flammable, or corrosive gases to keep food chilled. A faulty
compressor or leaky pipe could wipe out an entire family in their sleep, and in the first half of
1929, gas from fridges killed at least 15 people in Chicago alone.
Danger drove innovation, and in 1928, General Motors engineer Thomas Midgley Jr.
synthesized the first chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) — a cheap, non-toxic, non-flammable gas
marketed in the U.S. under the brand name Freon. CFCs seemed miraculous, and post-war
consumers fell in love with them. They became the coolant in every refrigerator and air
conditioner in the world, as well as the propellant of choice in billions of aerosol cans, ejecting
hairspray, deodorant, whipped cream, and countless other consumables, all at the push of a
button. But CFCs, the solution to an earlier problem, turned out to be villains in disguise. In
1974, University of California scientists F. Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina asked an
inconvenient question: Where do all the CFCs go?
Because CFC molecules are so stable, they don’t break down in the lower atmosphere.
Rowland and Molina hypothesized that they drifted upward into the stratosphere, 10 to 30
miles above the Earth’s surface, where they would be smashed apart by the Sun’s ultraviolet
(UV) rays. This releases chlorine atoms — like a microscopic, demented Pac-Man, a single one
can devour more than 100,000 ozone molecules.
If their hypothesis were correct, that would be catastrophic. The ozone layer is like Earth’s
sunscreen: It lets through most of the Sun’s relatively benign UV-A rays, absorbs most of the
harmful UV-B, and blocks all of the even more dangerous UV-C radiation. Without the ozone
layer, those unwelcome UV rays would reach Earth’s surface, where they'd mutate DNA,
cause skin cancers and cataracts, and kill crops and marine ecosystems. Fellow scientists were
skeptical of the theory, while the chemical industry was downright hostile. [Sci-Tech; Word
Count: 431]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://bigthink.com/strange-maps/ozone-
hole/

Environmental problems are solved mainly when industries voluntarily change their

backed.
Once a crisis is addressed, similar future crises become impossible to reoccur.

SECTION IV
XVI. In the late 20th century, the world came together to plug a hole in the ozone layer — the part
of Earth’s atmosphere that absorbs most of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet radiation. If left
unchecked, this hole would have exposed life on Earth to dangerous — and in some regions
potentially lethal — levels of radiation, but an international treaty brought us back from the
brink of disaster. That treaty, the Montreal Protocol, is a lesson in human resilience: We can
save the world, because we already did it once before.
The story of the Montreal Protocol starts, bizarrely, with an epidemic of deadly fridges in the
1920s. In those pioneer days of electric home refrigeration, everyone’s favorite new kitchen
appliance relied on highly toxic, flammable, or corrosive gases to keep food chilled. A faulty
compressor or leaky pipe could wipe out an entire family in their sleep, and in the first half of
1929, gas from fridges killed at least 15 people in Chicago alone.
Danger drove innovation, and in 1928, General Motors engineer Thomas Midgley Jr.
synthesized the first chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) — a cheap, non-toxic, non-flammable gas
marketed in the U.S. under the brand name Freon. CFCs seemed miraculous, and post-war
consumers fell in love with them. They became the coolant in every refrigerator and air
conditioner in the world, as well as the propellant of choice in billions of aerosol cans, ejecting
hairspray, deodorant, whipped cream, and countless other consumables, all at the push of a
button. But CFCs, the solution to an earlier problem, turned out to be villains in disguise. In
1974, University of California scientists F. Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina asked an
inconvenient question: Where do all the CFCs go?
Because CFC molecules are so stable, they don’t break down in the lower atmosphere.
Rowland and Molina hypothesized that they drifted upward into the stratosphere, 10 to 30
miles above the Earth’s surface, where they would be smashed apart by the Sun’s ultraviolet
(UV) rays. This releases chlorine atoms — like a microscopic, demented Pac-Man, a single one
can devour more than 100,000 ozone molecules.
If their hypothesis were correct, that would be catastrophic. The ozone layer is like Earth’s
sunscreen: It lets through most of the Sun’s relatively benign UV-A rays, absorbs most of the
harmful UV-B, and blocks all of the even more dangerous UV-C radiation. Without the ozone
layer, those unwelcome UV rays would reach Earth’s surface, where they'd mutate DNA,
cause skin cancers and cataracts, and kill crops and marine ecosystems. Fellow scientists were
skeptical of the theory, while the chemical industry was downright hostile. [Sci-Tech; Word
Count: 431]

XVII. On the foothills of the mountains, by the banks of the river in Cortina, there was a forest. It
was full of tall larch trees. Arborists said the oldest of them had been there for 150 years and
dendrologists that it was unique because it was unusual to find a monocultural forest growing
at such a low altitude in the southern Alps. The locals knew mostly it was the place where the
old wooden bobsleigh run was, where you went on your walks in summer or autumn, or when
you wanted to play tennis on the small courts built near the bottom. They called it the Bosco di
Ronco and it isn’t there anymore. Sustainability is the great lie of these Games. It was written
all through the bid document and the International Olympic Committee has slapped it across
all manner of promotional literature. www.lawpreptutorial.com
For the IOC, for sport in general, sustainability is a priority. If you want more details, the IOC
can give you any amount of information about its low carbon transport plan and how it is only
using recyclable cutlery and linen tablecloths. It will tell you over and again that 85% of the
venues being used at this Olympics already existed or are temporary.
What it won’t say is the vast majority of those existing venues needed to be demolished and
rebuilt with much larger footprints; that, for example, they decided to gouge a new snowpark
out of a mountain in Livigno even though they already had one at Trepalle in the adjacent
valley. Or that in Predazzo the ski jumps were rebuilt from scratch a few hundred metres

across from the existing ones. Or to make room for their new bobsleigh track they had to cut
down the Bosco di Ronco, so that, if you go there now, all you see is 2km of steel and concrete.
It won’t say, either, that the climate crisis has caused the average February temperatures in
Cortina to rise by 3.6C since the Olympics were last in Italy, 20 years ago, that the average
February snow depth has fallen by 15cm in the past 50 years and that they had to build four
high altitude reservoirs to provide the 2.3m cubic metres of artificial snow they need to fluff up
the ski runs to the required depth of 1.5m. Or that most of the water being used to fill those
reservoirs has to be pumped all the way up the mountains after being extracted from the local
rivers, which are already in drought for large parts of the year. [Environment; Word Count:
431]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from:
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/feb /22/the-great-olympic-lie-untold-story-of-
winter-games-huge-environmental-impact

XVII. The World Bank said India is well placed to weather the current global energy shock with
ample buffers, including high foreign exchange reserves, fiscal space and low inflation, which
will support growth despite global headwinds. Addressing a conference a day after raising
India's GDP growth projections for the current fiscal to 6.6 per cent, the World Bank said
India had dealt well the trade turbulence last fiscal and the Indian economy entered the
current Middle East crisis, which has led to volatility in oil markets, "from a position of
strength".
India has strong policy buffers, high Forex reserves, fiscal space, to provide support as needed,
as well as low inflation, and strong goals at the moment going into this current shock. And that
strong growth momentum is supported by gross positive policies, including the EU FTA and new
labour. All of these things, of course, reinforce and support strong growth momentum, and that's
fine. Despite the global headwinds, we do see India and the region continuing to be a very
strong, gross performing region compared to other emerging markets across the world. The
World Bank in its South Asia Economic Update report released on Wednesday, had said India's
growth is estimated to have accelerated from 7.1 per cent in FY25 to 7.6 per cent in FY26 (April
2025-March 2026), owing to strong domestic demand and export resilience. It projected growth
to slow to 6.6 per cent in FY27, but the projection is higher than 6.5 per cent made in the Global
Economic Prospects report released in January.
World Bank Lead Economist for India said India has remained the fastest-growing large
economy in the world in FY26, despite facing some of the highest tariffs on its exports globally.
He said the income tax cuts and GST rate reductions last year supported domestic
consumption, while exports and investment, areas which were expected to be adversely
affected by tariffs, performed much better than anticipated. India showed very strong
performance and resilience. Describing the current situation as a "major trade shock", the
World Bank said the risks to growth are tilted to the downside. The World Bank has assumed
oil price in FY27 at USD 90-100/ barrel for arriving at its growth estimates. The US-based
multilateral agency also appreciated the Indian government's strategy of handling that energy
crisis that emanated due to the Middle East conflict. [Economy; Word Count: 392]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from:
https: //economictimes.indiatimes.com/news /economy /indicators /india-has-ample-buffers-to-
weather-headwinds-from-middle-east-conflict-world-bank/articleshow/180139542.cms
content.questionText:
Which additional information would most strengthen the claim that India can absorb the
current energy shock without derailing growth?
options:
Unsecured consumer lending slowed after supervisors tightened norms, even as food
inflation eased across several states.

Rural real wages weakened while urban discretionary spending rose, indicating uneven
demand rather than broad macro resilience.

Reserve adequacy covers many months of imports and short-term external debt, enabling
smoother financing of pricier oil.

Portfolio inflows rose after investors rotated into emerging markets, but the shift was
driven by short-lived risk appetite.
content.explanation: The passage links resilience to the ability to withstand oil market volatility, which often becomes a problem through higher import bills and external financing needs. If reserves cover many months of imports and short-term external debt, it indicates stronger capacity to sustain essential payments during stress.

XXI. During the winter tourist season in Manali, three friends- Aarav, Meher, and Zubin- started a
temporary travel-essentials kiosk near a busy viewpoint. The stall sold woollen caps, gloves,
thermos bottles, and rain covers. Since the business was only for the season, they decided to
run it in partnership and keep proper records of their capital, time of investment, and profit-
sharing arrangement.
At the beginning of the season, Aarav invested 780,000 in the business. Meher joined the
business 2 months later with a capital of %1,00,000. Zubin also invested at the start, putting in
%1,20,000, but after 5 months he withdrew %30,000 from his capital and continued with the
reduced amount for the rest of the season. The business ran for a total of 12 months.
The partners agreed that before dividing the final profit, 10% of the total annual profit would
first be kept aside for stall rent, transport charges, and storage expenses. After this deduction,
36,000 would be given to Meher as a fixed management allowance because she handled
supplier calls, tourist group orders, and daily stock updates. The remaining profit would then
be divided among Aarav, Meher, and Zubin in the ratio of their effective capitals multiplied by
the time for which those capitals remained invested.www.lawpreptutorial.com
At the end of the season, the kiosk earned a total profit of %4,80,000. The partners then sat
together to calculate how much each one should receive and how the shares would change if
one partner had invested for a different period or changed capital midway.

temporary travel-essentials kiosk near a busy viewpoint. The stall sold woollen caps, gloves,
thermos bottles, and rain covers. Since the business was only for the season, they decided to
run it in partnership and keep proper records of their capital, time of investment, and profit-
sharing arrangement.
At the beginning of the season, Aarav invested 780,000 in the business. Meher joined the
business 2 months later with a capital of %1,00,000. Zubin also invested at the start, putting in
%1,20,000, but after 5 months he withdrew %30,000 from his capital and continued with the
reduced amount for the rest of the season. The business ran for a total of 12 months.
The partners agreed that before dividing the final profit, 10% of the total annual profit would
first be kept aside for stall rent, transport charges, and storage expenses. After this deduction,
36,000 would be given to Meher as a fixed management allowance because she handled
supplier calls, tourist group orders, and daily stock updates. The remaining profit would then
be divided among Aarav, Meher, and Zubin in the ratio of their effective capitals multiplied by
the time for which those capitals remained invested.www.lawpreptutorial.com
At the end of the season, the kiosk earned a total profit of %4,80,000. The partners then sat
together to calculate how much each one should receive and how the shares would change if
one partner had invested for a different period or changed capital midway.

SECTION I
L	The Economics was far from the only text of antiquity to tackle the question of home. First,
there was Xenophon’s book of the same name, written slightly before Aristotle’s, and slightly
less interesting. And later, Stoic writers took up the topic of the home with some enthusiasm,
writing about marriage, the family and the education of women. The most notable among
them were perhaps Musonius Rufus, a 1st-century CE Roman philosopher, and Hierocles the
Stoic, a 2nd-century CE Greek philosopher. Then there is the whole corpus of texts by a group
of philosophers known as the Neo-Pythagoreans, some signed by women, and many of them
discussing the home, women’s virtues and marital relations. The home, it turns out, was a
topic of considerable philosophical interest in antiquity.
Many of the fragments we have from Neo-Pythagorean writers who sign their texts with
women’s names concern the ethics and politics of domestic arrangements: what to do if your
husband cheats on you? How to deal with household slaves? Would a woman’s virtue enable
her, in principle, to rule a state? These texts are commonly rejected by studies of ancient
philosophers because they are hard to date, and quite likely written by writers using
pseudonyms. But they are philosophical texts written in antiquity, and they are about the
home, and I suspect that, if the home was regarded as a topic worthy of philosophical
interests, they would be read today. The Neo-Pythagorean authors are the subject of several
recent excellent and accessible books — eg, Pythagorean Women (2013) by Sarah Pomeroy,
Pythagorean Women Philosophers (2020) by Dorota Dutsch, PythagoreanWomen (2022) by
Caterina Pellé — so I would urge readers to consult these, and will now turn to Musonius and
Hierocles.
Musonius Rufus had his 15 minutes of fame some 25 years ago when Martha Nussbaum
noticed that he recommended women be educated as well as men. But while education does
matter to gender relations, so does the home, and Musonius, it turns out, has a lot to say about
that, as well as about education. First, he says that marriage is ‘community of life with a view
to the procreation of children’. Then he goes further and explores what married life should be
like, and what its legal and moral implications are. The marital ‘community’, he argues, must
be material and emotional: a husband and wife must regard ‘all things in common between
them, and nothing peculiar or private to one or the other, not even their own bodies.’ As well
as sharing their material possessions, they must share affection: there should be ‘above all
perfect companionship and mutual love of husband and wife’. If these conditions fail to obtain,
‘the union is doomed to disaster and though they live together, yet their common interests fare
badly’. [Word Count: 462]

domestic-life

them were perhaps Musonius Rufus, a 1st-century CE Roman philosopher, and Hierocles the
Stoic, a 2nd-century CE Greek philosopher. Then there is the whole corpus of texts by a group
of philosophers known as the Neo-Pythagoreans, some signed by women, and many of them
discussing the home, women’s virtues and marital relations. The home, it turns out, was a
topic of considerable philosophical interest in antiquity.
Many of the fragments we have from Neo-Pythagorean writers who sign their texts with
women’s names concern the ethics and politics of domestic arrangements: what to do if your
husband cheats on you? How to deal with household slaves? Would a woman’s virtue enable
her, in principle, to rule a state? These texts are commonly rejected by studies of ancient
philosophers because they are hard to date, and quite likely written by writers using
pseudonyms. But they are philosophical texts written in antiquity, and they are about the
home, and I suspect that, if the home was regarded as a topic worthy of philosophical
interests, they would be read today. The Neo-Pythagorean authors are the subject of several
recent excellent and accessible books — eg, Pythagorean Women (2013) by Sarah Pomeroy,
Pythagorean Women Philosophers (2020) by Dorota Dutsch, PythagoreanWomen (2022) by
Caterina Pellé — so I would urge readers to consult these, and will now turn to Musonius and
Hierocles.

noticed that he recommended women be educated as well as men. But while education does
matter to gender relations, so does the home, and Musonius, it turns out, has a lot to say about

I.	I cannot remember a time when I was not conscious of wealth. At the age of seven, attending a
private Quaker school in Cambridge, Massachusetts, I was embarrassed when wealthier
friends from the Boston suburbs came over to my house, which was small, compared with
theirs. Later, living in Arlington, Virginia, and at a public school, I felt the opposite: sheepish
about a house that was grander than some of my friends’ homes. House size was one of the
earliest metrics by which I clocked wealth.
Wealth was always something I quietly wrestled with. My father grew up in a poor farming
family, but my mother came from money: her father was an early billionaire. Though I was
raised materially as middle class, my own identity has had influxes from both extremes of the
class circumstances into which my parents were born — inheriting a confidence and
adventurousness, even feelings of invincibility, that come with privilege; while also tapping
into the thriftiness, stoic resilience and determination that come from bootstrapping.
My grandfather, who never questioned his standing, pursued wealth with singular dedication.
My early memories of him are anchored in his country estate in Millbrook, New York; I caught
salamanders by the pool; visited the kennels where he kept hunting dogs; caviar was regularly
served with dinner. Though he’s now in his 90s, his shadow looms large — as a patriarch who

scandalised his WASPy beach club in Southampton with his European Speedos, competed in
every endeavour (even beating my brother and me at backgammon as children), and whom
others craned to impress, though he lived very privately. [Word Count: 266]

Ill.	As an unbaptised agnostic raised with no religion, the closest I ever really come to a spiritual
experience is when I’m standing in front of an artwork. Last week I went to Florence to do
exactly that, drawn there not by Michelangelo’s David or Botticelli’s Birth of Venus, but by the
works of Mark Rothko, that titan of US abstract expressionism whose work seems, on the
surface at least, distinctly secular and un-Florentine. Yet seeing Renaissance art there had a
profound impact on Rothko and his painting, as the exhibition Rothko in Florence makes
strikingly explicit. Taking place at Palazzo Strozzi and two other satellite sites, it has been
curated by his son, Christopher, and the author and independent curator Elena Geuna.
Is it embarrassing to admit that when confronted with the first large canvas I was drawn to I
felt tearful? It was an emotion born of appreciation and astonishment but also — and this
startled me — a feeling of gratitude. I felt profoundly lucky to be there, in front of this painting,
not long after a time in my life where for various reasons I had not been feeling all that

fortunate at all. To have the chance to take in the paint on the monumental canvas, and
absorb the ways the colours — purples, reds, oranges, yellows, blues — blend and in places seem
to glow felt hugely significant to me personally. And then, as I continued to look — and as ever
with Rothko —I stopped thinking about myself at all.
That’s the beauty of his art, especially in these self-referential times: the way it encourages
the identity to break down and dissolve in the face of its contemplation. In that sense, its
underpinnings are not so different from those of religious art; in this casting off of the self,
then comes awe and wonder.www.lawpreptutorial.com
It is art as meditation, as secular worship. I felt it especially the next day at the former San
Marco monastery, where the cells were frescoed by the great Fra Angelico with religious
scenes for the private contemplation and worship of each monk. Rothko was overwhelmed
when he saw these, having finally got to Florence aged 47, and wanted his own colour field
paintings to provoke a similarly intense, spiritual response. [Word Count: 376]

monumental-florence-exhibition-renaissance-religious-art

IV.	Having gone quiet for a few months since lockdown, the reliably informative Exhibition on
Screen series returns with a profile of Frida Kahlo, the Mexican painter who has long been
venerated as a pioneer of feminist iconography as well as a champion of the country’s
indigenous culture. While the series tends to use large-scale exhibitions as a cue, this film
spends only brief periods inside a gallery spaces — primarily the Museo Dolores Olmedo in
Mexico City, which holds significant amounts of Kahlo’s work, as well as her husband’s Diego
Rivera. Instead, we get a straightforward, meat-and-potatoes overview of Kahlo’s life,
peppered with copious commentary from the usual top-notch academic and curatorial talent,
as well as family members.
While it’s perhaps not fair to make grandiose claims for this sober-toned film, I suspect it’s
trying to somehow reclaim the artist from “Fridamania”, the surge of admiration that swept
the cultural world in the 70s and 80s when Kahlo’s preoccupations — her brutal physical
realities, the adoption of costume and imagery, the use of her body as a personal theatre —
became fashionable, decades after her death. There’s a measured tone throughout, as well as
some great photographs: Kahlo with Rivera, who always seems to look as if he’s just woken up;
Kahlo’s father, whose spiffy goatee is surely the source of the shadowy facial hair Kahlo liked
to paint on to herself; and Kahlo herself as a radiant teenager and twentysomething, despite
the horrific bus crash that affected her from the age of 18.
Though necessarily a little light on detail, this is a film that covers the required bases, striking
a good balance between Kahlo’s often dramatic personal life and the ins and outs of her artistic
achievements. (A fervent case is made that Kahlo was the first artist to render menstrual
blood on canvas, in her heartbreaking depiction of her miscarriage and hospital stay in
Detroit, where she had accompanied Rivera on one of his mural commissions.)
There’s also an interesting sidebar on Mexican retablo painting — the votive street art that is
still a traditional method of attempting to gain divine intercession — which Kahlo herself
collected and which was a clear influence on her own work. All in all, a very watchable film
about an ever-intriguing figure. [Word Count: 376]

IV.	Having gone quiet for a few months since lockdown, the reliably informative Exhibition on
Screen series returns with a profile of Frida Kahlo, the Mexican painter who has long been
venerated as a pioneer of feminist iconography as well as a champion of the country’s
indigenous culture. While the series tends to use large-scale exhibitions as a cue, this film
spends only brief periods inside a gallery spaces — primarily the Museo Dolores Olmedo in
Mexico City, which holds significant amounts of Kahlo’s work, as well as her husband’s Diego
Rivera. Instead, we get a straightforward, meat-and-potatoes overview of Kahlo’s life,
peppered with copious commentary from the usual top-notch academic and curatorial talent,
as well as family members.
While it’s perhaps not fair to make grandiose claims for this sober-toned film, I suspect it’s
trying to somehow reclaim the artist from “Fridamania”, the surge of admiration that swept
the cultural world in the 70s and 80s when Kahlo’s preoccupations — her brutal physical
realities, the adoption of costume and imagery, the use of her body as a personal theatre —
became fashionable, decades after her death. There’s a measured tone throughout, as well as
some great photographs: Kahlo with Rivera, who always seems to look as if he’s just woken up;
Kahlo’s father, whose spiffy goatee is surely the source of the shadowy facial hair Kahlo liked
to paint on to herself; and Kahlo herself as a radiant teenager and twentysomething, despite
the horrific bus crash that affected her from the age of 18.
Though necessarily a little light on detail, this is a film that covers the required bases, striking
a good balance between Kahlo’s often dramatic personal life and the ins and outs of her artistic
achievements. (A fervent case is made that Kahlo was the first artist to render menstrual
blood on canvas, in her heartbreaking depiction of her miscarriage and hospital stay in
Detroit, where she had accompanied Rivera on one of his mural commissions.)
There’s also an interesting sidebar on Mexican retablo painting — the votive street art that is
still a traditional method of attempting to gain divine intercession — which Kahlo herself
collected and which was a clear influence on her own work. All in all, a very watchable film
about an ever-intriguing figure. [Word Count: 376]

possible — and rapidly bring temperatures back down.

towards renewables — the only sustainable path to lower costs and to real energy security.
Cutting methane — one of the fastest, cheapest ways to limit near-term warming. Protecting
forests, land, and seas. Helping communities adapt to the devastating impacts already here.
And it means fulfilling climate finance promises to developing countries — to save lives, protect
livelihoods, and strengthen economies, he added. This is the moment to act — for our
environment and for our future. As our planet continues to face the devastating impacts of
climate change, the science is clear. [Word Count: 252]

VI.	Seeking to expand cooperation and technology-sharing in the realm, India and the United
Kingdom formally launched the Critical Minerals Global Supply Chain Observatory (GSCO).
The observatory was first announced during U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s visit to India
in October last year to “expand mineral coverage, further integrate advanced technologies and
unlock new bilateral investment opportunities”.
The platform — to be jointly operated by India’s Technology Innovation in Exploration &
Mining Foundation (TEXMiN), Indian Institute of Technology (ISM) Dhanbad and U.K.’s
University of Cambridge — will institute a data-driven platform to monitor and analyse global
critical mineral supply chains
Union Minister for Coal and Mines G. Kishan Reddy expressed that , This is a major step
towards strengthening critical mineral supply chains, supporting clean energy transitions, and

building resilient global supply chains through the India—U.K. partnership. U.K.’s Foreign
Secretary Yvette Cooper emphasised greater access to critical minerals and improved
information-sharing would be mutually beneficial to both countries.
According to the announcement readout, Ms. Cooper also stated the observatory could also
serve “as a foundation for broader cooperation across the critical minerals sector and related
strategic industries. Addressing the gathering, Shri G. Kishan Reddy emphasized that critical
minerals are the backbone of modern economies and indispensable for clean energy
technologies, advanced manufacturing, electric mobility and strategic sectors. He noted that
the Observatory would strengthen India's capabilities in critical mineral supply chain
intelligence, support evidence-based policymaking, and advance the objectives of the National
Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM).
[Word Count: 244]
