VI.	Seeking to expand cooperation and technology-sharing in the realm, India and the United
Kingdom formally launched the Critical Minerals Global Supply Chain Observatory (GSCO).
The observatory was first announced during U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s visit to India
in October last year to “expand mineral coverage, further integrate advanced technologies and
unlock new bilateral investment opportunities”.
The platform — to be jointly operated by India’s Technology Innovation in Exploration &
Mining Foundation (TEXMiN), Indian Institute of Technology (ISM) Dhanbad and U.K.’s
University of Cambridge — will institute a data-driven platform to monitor and analyse global
critical mineral supply chains
Union Minister for Coal and Mines G. Kishan Reddy expressed that , This is a major step
towards strengthening critical mineral supply chains, supporting clean energy transitions, and

building resilient global supply chains through the India—U.K. partnership. U.K.’s Foreign
Secretary Yvette Cooper emphasised greater access to critical minerals and improved
information-sharing would be mutually beneficial to both countries.
According to the announcement readout, Ms. Cooper also stated the observatory could also
serve “as a foundation for broader cooperation across the critical minerals sector and related
strategic industries. Addressing the gathering, Shri G. Kishan Reddy emphasized that critical
minerals are the backbone of modern economies and indispensable for clean energy
technologies, advanced manufacturing, electric mobility and strategic sectors. He noted that
the Observatory would strengthen India's capabilities in critical mineral supply chain
intelligence, support evidence-based policymaking, and advance the objectives of the National
Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM).

diversifies funding sources to support maritime and coastal infrastructure development.
Globally, just over $15 billion in blue bonds had been issued by mid-2025, according to World
Bank data.
India’s benchmark 10-year yield has risen around 35 basis points since the start of the U.S.-
Iran war, denting activity in the bond market. The company plans to raise as much as 7100
billion in financial year 2027 to finance projects that strengthen India’s maritime ecosystem,
including greenfield and brownfield ports, last-mile port connectivity, shipbuilding, inland
waterways and coastal road networks. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The company also administers the government’s %250-billion Maritime Development Fund,
which includes a 2%50-billion Interest Incentivisation Fund, allowing it to provide interest
subsidies to borrowers. It is also seeking a %20-billion equity infusion from the government to
maintain a healthy debt-to-equity ratio as it expands its loan book.
Global climate change has impacted India’s coastline ecosystem with rising sea levels and
more devastating cyclones, impacting the coastal economy and the lives of millions of
inhabitants in the coastal belt. This moment of truth poses a critical question to the world’s
fastest-growing $ 4.13 trillion Indian economy: How will it finance the infrastructure needed
to protect 250 million coastal residents while preserving marine ecosystems that underpin a
$7 billion seafood export industry? The answer may lie in an innovative financial instrument
that may prove to be a game -changer to build a sustainable finance ecosystem: the blue
bonds. [Word Count: 250]

VIII. The annual NITI Aayog meeting, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has in recent
years been marked by boycotts and absences from several chief ministers, particularly those
heading opposition-ruled states. This year, however, broke that trend. Chief ministers from all
28 states attended the country's apex public policy forum on Thursday, making it one of the
most widely attended editions of the council in the recent past.
The 11th Governing Council meeting, held at the Rashtrapati Bhavan Cultural Centre, saw
the participation of chief ministers from all seven opposition-ruled states -- Tamil Nadu's
Joseph Vijay, Karnataka's DK Shivakumar, Kerala's VD Satheesan, Telangana's Revanth
Reddy, Jharkhand's Hemant Soren, Himachal Pradesh's Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu and
Jammu and Kashmir's Omar Abdullah. They were joined by BJP chief ministers, including
Devendra Fadnavis, Yogi Adityanath and Suvendu Adhikari among others.
In addition to the chief ministers, the Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories and several
Union ministers attended the meeting. The event, tasked with shaping national priorities and

development strategies through active cooperation between the Centre and states, recorded a
level of participation not seen in recent years.
Following the NITI Aayog meeting, the chief ministers of Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu,
Karnataka, Telangana and Jammu and Kashmir met Prime Minister Modi individually. Four
of these states are governed by opposition parties. Last year, three opposition chief ministers —
West Bengal's Mamata Banerjee, Kerala's Pinarayi Vijayan, and Karnataka's Siddaramaiah —
along with NDA ally Bihar Chief Minister Nitish Kumar, skipped the 10th Governing Council
meeting. [Word Count: 246]

IX.	India spent $92.1 billion on its military in 2025 according to a new report by the Stockholm
International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI). That is 8.9 per cent more than what India
spent the year before.
Countries around the world spent a record $2.9 trillion on their militaries in 2025 — equal to
2.5% of the entire world's economic output. This is the eleventh consecutive year that global
military spending has increased, and the highest figure SIPRI has ever recorded since it began
tracking in 1949.
SIPRI listed the India-Pakistan clash as one of the most dangerous flashpoints of the year.
The report said India struck Pakistani air and missile bases — some of which are believed to
have nuclear-related roles — but noted that “both sides took steps to avoid escalation. The
report also pointed out that it was the first time India and Pakistan openly used cyberattacks
as part of an armed conflict. In its timeline of major events for the year, SIPRI recorded: May
7-10: India and Pakistan exchange intense cross-border fire.
International transfers of major arms reached their highest level since the end of the Cold War
during 2021-25, marking a 9.2% increase compared to 2016-20. USA, France, Russia,
Germany and China accounted for 70 per cent of export of arms. India was the second largest
recipient of major arms between 2021-25, accounting for 8.2 % in Global arms import. India is
believed to have slightly expanded its nuclear stockpile in 2025 and continued developing new

content.questionText:
Meera is the natural guardian of her 14-year-old son, Rahul, who owns an undeveloped and
undivided share in a piece of agricultural land. Facing a severe financial crisis due to Rahul’s
sudden, urgent medical emergency and pending school fees, Meera decides to liquidate this
asset. She sells a small portion of this undivided share to a local buyer at the exact market
price. The village elders formally approve the sale, and every rupee is directly used to pay the
hospital and the school. No prior permission of the court is obtained because Meera believed
the clear benefit to her son justified the quick sale. Can this sale transaction be legally
justified solely on the ground that it was necessary and beneficial to the minor?
options:
Yes, because a natural guardian has the legal authority to manage a minor's estate and
can convert an unproductive asset into usable funds for the child's urgent welfare.

Yes, because the combination of fair market value, local village approval, and the actual
use of money proves that the best interest of the child was fully protected.

No, because the law strictly requires prior court permission for transferring a minor's
immovable property, which cannot be bypassed even for genuine welfare reasons.

No, because any transfer of a minor's immovable property executed without prior judicial
approval is void from the beginning and has no legal effect.
content.explanation: the passage explicitly provides that a natural guardian cannot sell or transfer any part of the minor’s immovable property without prior permission of the court. Even though the Shephali Chakraborty case notes that converting an undeveloped, undivided share into usable funds can be a genuine benefit, such a realistic evaluation must be made by the court before the sale, making the unilateral transaction legally unjustified.

years after he reaches adulthood. Is prior court permission required for this lease?

No, because the total duration of the lease is under five years and stays within the

for protecting the minor’s property.

A district court appoints Nirmal as guardian of a 12-year-old ward’s immovable property.
Nirmal later mortgages part of the ward’s land to raise money for repairs to another property
belonging to the ward. He obtains written approval from the ward’s maternal uncle, a local
welfare officer, and two village elders, but does not seek permission from the court that
appointed him. When the mortgage is questioned, Nirmal argues that these approvals were
sufficient because responsible persons had considered the ward’s interest. Is this argument
legally sustainable?
options:
Yes, because a guardian may execute transactions that are necessary, reasonable, and
proper for managing the ward’s estate.

Yes, because approvals from family elders and a welfare officer sufficiently protect the
ward under parens patriae.

No, because a court-appointed guardian cannot mortgage the ward’s immovable property
without prior court permission.

No, because repairing another property can not amount to a necessary or clearly
advantageous transaction for the ward.

XI.	In a significant decision on the scope of compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the
Supreme Court considered whether injuries caused by the fall of a roadside tree branch on a
stationary autorickshaw could be treated as an accident “arising out of the use of a motor
vehicle”. The claimant was travelling in an autorickshaw in Bengaluru when heavy rain forced
him to stop by the roadside. While the vehicle was standing under an old tree, a branch fell on
it and caused grievous injuries, including permanent paraplegia.
The main provision considered was Section 165 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. This section
empowers the State Government to constitute Motor Accident Claims Tribunals for deciding
compensation claims arising from accidents involving death, bodily injury, or damage to third-
party property. However, the accident must arise out of the use of a motor vehicle. Therefore,
the Tribunal’s jurisdiction depends not merely on the presence of a vehicle, but on a real
connection between the injury and the use of that vehicle. Section 166 of the Act provides the
procedural route for filing an application for compensation in such cases. A claim under this
section must relate to an accident of the kind described in Section 165. Hence, where the
injury is caused by an external event having no proximate connection with the vehicle’s
movement, operation, condition, or use, Section 166 may not be the proper remedy. The Court
acknowledged that the expression “use of a motor vehicle” has been interpreted broadly. It can
include cases where the vehicle is stationary and not moving. Similarly, the phrase “arising

Four persons file applications under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act after suffering
injuries in different situations.

thrown against the metal railing inside the bus.

tree falls during a storm and crushes the roof.
iv. Charu is injured when a truck’s worn-out tyre bursts while the truck is carrying goods,
causing the truck to overturn.

166 provides the procedural route?
options: Claims i, ii and iv only.
Claims i, iii and iv only.
Claims ii, iii and iv only.
Claims i, ii and iii only.

Rukmini’s injury is connected to braking during bus travel, Farhan’s injury is connected to the unloading use of the delivery van and its ramp, and Charu’s injury is connected to the truck’s worn-out tyre while carrying goods.

Amit is travelling in a taxi from Bhopal railway station to his office. Heavy rain causes traffic
to stop beneath a flyover. The taxi driver switches off the engine and parks at the extreme left
of the road to wait for the rain to reduce. While waiting, Amit steps out of the taxi to answer a
phone call, remaining beside the vehicle. At that moment, a large advertising signboard fixed
to the flyover above becomes detached due to poor maintenance and falls directly on Amit,
causing serious injuries. The taxi had no defect, did not strike any object, and nothing
connected with its movement, operation or condition contributed to the signboard falling. Amit
files a claim under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, arguing that he was still in the
course of the same journey and had stepped out only briefly. Is Section 166 the proper remedy
on these facts?
options:
Yes, because Amit's journey had not ended and the injury occurred while he remained
connected with the ongoing use of the taxi.

Yes, because Amit had stepped out only temporarily and the vehicle continued to be part of
the same transport activity.

No, because the injury resulted from an external event lacking a proximate connection
with the taxi's movement, operation, condition or use.

No, because compensation under Section 166 is confined to injuries suffered while a
claimant remains physically inside the motor vehicle.
‘SCAN the QR for T&Cs
content.explanation: the signboard collapsed due to an independent external event. The passage explains that where the injury lacks a proximate connection with the vehicle's movement, operation, condition or use, Section 166 may not be the appropriate remedy.

content.questionText:
Sonal is waiting in a parked car beside a public road while her driver buys fuel coupons from a
nearby counter. A temporary festival arch erected by private organisers collapses during
strong winds and falls on the car, injuring Sonal. The car was insured, but it had no defect, did
not move, and did not hit the arch or its supporting ropes. Sonal files a claim before the Claims
Tribunal. The Tribunal records that the collapse of the arch had no connection with the
movement, operation, condition or use of the car, but still awards compensation against the
car’s insurer under Section 168, stating that it has the power to determine compensation and
specify the person who must pay. What is the likely legal position under the stated principles?
options:
The award may stand because Section 168 empowers the Tribunal to determine
compensation and name the payer.

The award may stand because the injury occurred in a public place while Sonal was seated
in an insured car.

The award is vulnerable because Section 168 requires proof that the owner personally
caused the injury.

The award is vulnerable because Section 168 applies after the case falls within the Motor
Vehicles Act.
content.explanation: the statutory requirement of a motor-vehicle accident is absent on the Tribunal’s own finding. Section 168 cannot create liability where the case does not first fall within the Motor Vehicles Act.

content.questionText:
Rekha is travelling in an insured city bus on a permitted route. During a lawful halt at a
traffic signal, the driver keeps the bus stationary with the doors closed. A dispute between two
groups breaks out on the roadside, and an unknown person throws a stone at the other group.
The stone misses its target, enters the bus through an open window, and injures Rekha. The
bus had no defect, did not strike anyone or anything, and its movement, operation or condition
did not contribute to the stone being thrown. Rekha files a claim against the bus insurer,
arguing that she was injured while travelling in an insured motor vehicle in a public place. Is
the insurer liable under the stated principles?
options:
Yes, because Rekha was a passenger in an insured bus during a halt in the course of public
transport.

Yes, because the injury occurred inside the bus while it was being used on a permitted
public route.

No, because insurer liability arises only when the vehicle collides with another person or
object.
No, because the injury resulted from an external act without any causal role of the bus.
content.explanation: the stone was thrown by an unknown person during a roadside dispute, and the bus had no role in causing or contributing to that act. The passage requires that the injury be caused by, or arise out of, the use of the vehicle; mere presence inside the insured bus is insufficient.

Karan is sitting inside an insured car parked near a public park during heavy rain. The driver
has stopped because visibility is poor. A large branch from an old roadside tree suddenly
breaks during a strong gust of wind and falls on the car, injuring Karan. The car had no
defect, did not hit the tree, and its position did not contribute to the branch falling.
Assertion (A): Karan’s claim against the motor insurer should not succeed merely because he
was injured while sitting inside an insured car.
Reason (R): A motor accident claim still requires a meaningful link between the injury and
the use of the vehicle, and an unforeseen natural event may weaken that link on the facts.

content.passageText:
XII. Wrongful restraint and wrongful confinement are offences against personal liberty and
freedom of movement. Article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution protects the right of citizens to move
freely throughout India, while Article 21 protects personal liberty. Criminal law gives effect to
these guarantees by punishing unlawful obstruction or detention. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023, wrongful restraint is dealt with under Section 126 and wrongful confinement
under Section 127.
Wrongful restraint occurs when a person voluntarily obstructs another person so as to prevent
that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed. The
obstruction may be physical, verbal, threatening, or created by circumstances, provided it
unlawfully prevents movement. The essence of the offence is that the victim must have a legal
right to move in that direction, and the accused must voluntarily obstruct that movement.
Mere advice, request, or moral pressure will not amount to wrongful restraint unless it
effectively prevents lawful movement.
The law also recognises an exception. If a person, in good faith, believes that he has a lawful
right to obstruct a private way over land or water, such obstruction does not amount to
wrongful restraint. However, the belief must be genuine and connected with a private way;
obstruction of a public road or obstruction without lawful basis cannot claim this protection.
Wrongful confinement is a more serious and narrower form of wrongful restraint. It occurs
when a person wrongfully restrains another in such a manner as to prevent that person from
proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits. In wrongful restraint, movement is blocked
only in one or some directions; in wrongful confinement, the person is prevented from moving
beyond a fixed boundary. Thus, all wrongful confinement involves restraint, but every
wrongful restraint is not confinement. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Actual physical force is not always necessary for wrongful confinement. Locking a person in a
room, surrounding exits with guards, threatening immediate violence if the person leaves, or

creating a reasonable fear that escape is impossible may amount to confinement. The test is
whether the person’s liberty to leave the defined area has been unlawfully curtailed.
The seriousness of wrongful confinement increases with duration and purpose. Section 127
punishes ordinary wrongful confinement, confinement for three days or more, confinement for
ten days or more, secret confinement, confinement after a writ of release has been issued, and
confinement for extortion of property, confession, or illegal compulsion. These aggravated
forms show that the law treats prolonged, secret, coercive, or extortion-based confinement
more seriously. [Word Count: 415]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://blog.ipleaders.in/wrongful-restraint-
wrongful-confinement

Nisha is accused by a shop owner of switching a costly watch with a duplicate. The shop owner
asks her to wait until the police arrive. The front exit is left open, but two employees stand
near it and repeatedly say that if she steps out, they will “break her phone and drag her back.”
Nisha remains seated for two hours. The owner later argues that no confinement occurred
because no one touched her and the exit was technically open. Is this argument legally
sustainable?
options:
Yes, because an open exit prevents wrongful confinement unless the victim is locked inside
a space or subjected to continuous physical restraint.

Yes, because remaining in a commercial establishment during a theft dispute constitutes a
voluntary stay rather than an unlawful curtailment of liberty.

No, because a shop owner's suspicion of theft automatically invalidates the requirement to
prove that the victim's physical movement was restricted.

No, because the deployment of employees combined with threats of immediate force can
cause a reasonable apprehension that leaving the area is impossible.

The officer’s conduct is justified because Rajeev was moved to a different location after the

The detention raises legal concerns because it continued despite a writ of release and his

content.passageText:
XIII. The doctrine of colourable legislation is an important constitutional principle used to examine
whether a legislature has acted within the limits of its law-making power. It is based on the
maxim that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. A legislature may appear
to make a law within its authority, but if the real substance of the law enters a field beyond its
constitutional competence, the law may be treated as colourable legislation.
In India, legislative powers are distributed mainly through Articles 245 and 246 of the
Constitution and the Seventh Schedule. Article 245(1) provides that, subject to the
Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India, and a State
Legislature may make laws for the whole or any part of that State. Article 245(2) provides that
a law made by Parliament shall not be invalid merely because it has extra-territorial
operation.
Article 246 deals with the subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and State Legislatures.
Article 246(1) gives Parliament exclusive power to make laws on matters in List I, known as
the Union List. Article 246(2) allows both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws on
matters in List III, known as the Concurrent List. Article 246(3) gives State Legislatures
exclusive power to make laws on matters in List II, known as the State List, subject to
Parliament’s powers under clauses (1) and (2). Article 246(4) allows Parliament to legislate for
any part of India not included in a State, even on matters in the State List.
If a legislature makes a law on a subject assigned to another legislature, it acts beyond its
competence. The doctrine prevents a legislature from disguising such an encroachment by
giving the law an appearance of validity. Courts do not depend merely on the title, form, or
language of the law. They examine the true nature, object, and effect of the legislation.
If the substance of the law falls within the legislature’s field, the law is valid even if it
incidentally affects another field. However, if the substance of the law belongs to an
unauthorised field, it cannot be saved merely because its wording appears lawful.
Colourable legislation is sometimes described as a fraud on the Constitution. This does not
mean dishonest intention. In constitutional law, the focus is on legislative competence, not
personal motive. If the legislature has no power to enact a law, its intention or policy reason
cannot make the law valid. [Word Count: 409]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://lawbhoomi.com/doctrine-of-
colourable-legislation/

that its purpose is to maintain public order and prevent unrest caused by misleading online
content. The Act requires every social media platform operating anywhere in India to obtain a
licence from State X if its posts are accessible to users in State X. It also empowers State X
authorities to suspend accounts of users located in other States if their posts are likely to
affect public sentiment in State X. The State defends the law as a reasonable restriction
necessary to balance free expression with public order. A platform headquartered and
operating mainly outside State X challenges the Act as colourable legislation. Which
conclusion is most appropriate?
options:
The law is valid because public order justifies a reasonable restriction on online expression
affecting State X residents.

The law is valid because the title and stated object show that State X is acting within its
public-order concern.

The law may be invalid because constitutional balancing cannot save a law whose real
substance enters a field beyond competence.

The law may be invalid if the platform proves that State X acted with dishonest political or
personal motive.

content.passageText:
XIII. The doctrine of colourable legislation is an important constitutional principle used to examine
whether a legislature has acted within the limits of its law-making power. It is based on the
maxim that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. A legislature may appear
to make a law within its authority, but if the real substance of the law enters a field beyond its
constitutional competence, the law may be treated as colourable legislation.
In India, legislative powers are distributed mainly through Articles 245 and 246 of the
Constitution and the Seventh Schedule. Article 245(1) provides that, subject to the
Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India, and a State
Legislature may make laws for the whole or any part of that State. Article 245(2) provides that
a law made by Parliament shall not be invalid merely because it has extra-territorial
operation.
Article 246 deals with the subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and State Legislatures.
Article 246(1) gives Parliament exclusive power to make laws on matters in List I, known as
the Union List. Article 246(2) allows both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws on
matters in List III, known as the Concurrent List. Article 246(3) gives State Legislatures
exclusive power to make laws on matters in List II, known as the State List, subject to
Parliament’s powers under clauses (1) and (2). Article 246(4) allows Parliament to legislate for
any part of India not included in a State, even on matters in the State List.
If a legislature makes a law on a subject assigned to another legislature, it acts beyond its
competence. The doctrine prevents a legislature from disguising such an encroachment by
giving the law an appearance of validity. Courts do not depend merely on the title, form, or
language of the law. They examine the true nature, object, and effect of the legislation.
If the substance of the law falls within the legislature’s field, the law is valid even if it
incidentally affects another field. However, if the substance of the law belongs to an
unauthorised field, it cannot be saved merely because its wording appears lawful.
Colourable legislation is sometimes described as a fraud on the Constitution. This does not
mean dishonest intention. In constitutional law, the focus is on legislative competence, not
personal motive. If the legislature has no power to enact a law, its intention or policy reason
cannot make the law valid. [Word Count: 409]

colourable-legislation/

territory that is part of India but is not included in any State. The Act regulates local

and India-registered companies that operate fraudulent investment schemes from foreign

disclose foreign bank accounts connected with the scheme. A company incorporated in India
but operating from Singapore challenges the Act, arguing that Parliament cannot make a law

No, because a law made by Parliament does not become invalid on the ground that it has
extra-territorial operation.

XIV. Bailment is a special contract recognised under Sections 148 to 171 of the Indian Contract Act,
1872. Section 148 defines bailment as delivery of goods by one person to another for some
purpose, upon a contract that the goods shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned
or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. The person
delivering the goods is called the bailor, and the person receiving them is called the bailee.
The essence of bailment is delivery of possession, not transfer of ownership. The bailee
receives temporary possession and must use the goods only for the agreed purpose. Bailment
may arise through express contract, implied contract, or even by operation of law, such as
where a person finds goods belonging to another and assumes responsibility over them.
Section 149 recognises that delivery may be made by doing anything which has the effect of
putting the goods in the possession of the intended bailee.
The bailor has important duties. Under Section 150, the bailor must disclose faults in the
goods which are known to him and which materially interfere with their use or expose the
bailee to extraordinary risk. If the bailor fails to disclose such faults, he is responsible for
damage caused to the bailee. In gratuitous bailment, this duty applies to known faults; in non-
gratuitous bailment, the responsibility is stricter.
The bailee must take reasonable care of the goods. Section 151 requires the bailee to take as
much care of the goods as a person of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods. Under
Section 152, if such care is taken, the bailee is not responsible for loss, destruction, or
deterioration of the goods, unless there is a special contract. However, under Sections 153 and
154, unauthorised use of the goods may terminate the bailment and make the bailee liable for
loss arising from such use.
The bailee must return or deliver the goods according to the bailor’s directions when the
purpose is accomplished or the time of bailment expires. Under Section 161, if the bailee

defaults in returning the goods, he becomes responsible for any loss, destruction, or
deterioration from that time. The bailee must also return any increase or profit from the goods
under Section 163, unless agreed otherwise.
The bailee has rights too. He may claim necessary expenses in gratuitous bailment under
Section 158, compensation for defective title under Section 164, and lien under Sections 170
and 171. A pledge under Section 172 is a special form of bailment where goods are delivered as
security for debt or performance of a promise.
[Word Count: 434]

bailment/

Aarav gives his vintage motorcycle to Bhavesh, a mechanic, for three days so that Bhavesh can
test the engine and identify its defects. Aarav explicitly instructs Bhavesh that once the defect
is identified, Bhavesh must either return the motorcycle to Aarav or deliver it directly to a
third-party specialist, but the transfer to the specialist can only happen if Aarav gives a
separate approval later. Bhavesh subsequently argues that a valid contract of bailment was
never created because Aarav’s instructions left the final disposal of the motorcycle entirely
unsettled and conditional upon a future approval. Is Bhavesh’s argument legally sustainable?
options:
Yes, because a contract of bailment cannot be legally sustained when the final disposal of
the goods depends entirely on a future, unsettled approval.

Yes, because Aarav's conditional instruction to send the motorcycle to a third-party
specialist prevents a definitive, immediate obligation to return the goods to the original
bailor.

No, because the motorcycle was delivered for a specific testing purpose with clear
directions regarding its return or conditional further disposal.

No, because the later approval requirement delayed disposal and gave Bhavesh discretion
to choose the next course after testing.

Kavya owns expensive lighting equipment kept in a locked studio. She agrees to let Rohan use
the equipment for a wedding shoot. Instead of physically handing over each item, Kavya gives
Rohan the studio access code, disables her own lock, and instructs the security guard to allow
only Rohan to remove the equipment. Before Rohan removes anything, a dispute arises, and
Kavya claims there was no delivery because the goods were not handed over physically. Is
Kavya’s claim correct?
options: Yes, because delivery under bailment requires physical handing over of each movable item.
Yes, because Rohan had permission to enter but had not yet removed the goods.
No, because Kavya’s acts placed the goods in Rohan’s effective possession.
No, because intention creates bailment even before possession is affected.

agreed delivery route, which includes a slope, and suffers injuries when the brake sensor fails.
Tushar argues that he is not responsible because Abhishek voluntarily accepted the scooter
and used it carefully. Is Tushar liable for the damage?
options: Yes, because Tushar knew of a fault that exposed Abhishek to extraordinary risk.
Yes, because a bailor is liable for every defect discovered after delivery.
No, because Abhishek accepted an old scooter and used it for his own work.

content.questionText:
Meera leaves an antique wooden chest with Nikhil, a professional storage operator, for two
months while her house is renovated. Nikhil keeps the chest in the same humidity-controlled
room where he stores his own expensive furniture, checks the room daily, and maintains
security records. During an unexpected internal wiring spark, the sprinkler system damages
the chest. Meera argues that Nikhil must compensate her because the chest deteriorated while
it was in his possession.
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Nikhil’s duty is to take the level of care that an ordinarily prudent person
would take of his own goods.
Statement B: Nikhil becomes liable merely because the chest deteriorated while it was in his
custody.
Statement C: The comparison is with reasonable ordinary care, not with perfect protection
against every mishap.
Which of the above statements is correct?
options: Statements A and C are correct, while Statement B applies an excessive standard.
Statements A and B are correct, while Statement C reduces the bailee’s duty.
Statements B and C are correct, while Statement A ignores professional storage.
Statement A alone is correct, while Statements B and C excuse deterioration.
content.explanation: the passage states that the bailee’s duty is measured by the care of a person of ordinary prudence dealing with his own goods. Nikhil stored the chest with precautions similar to those used for his own valuable furniture, and the standard is reasonable care, not faultless preservation.

Harshita leaves a rare musical instrument with Priyanshu for repair and explicitly requests him to
return it by Monday evening because it is required for a recorded performance on Tuesday.
Priyanshu completes the necessary repair work on Monday morning but intentionally retains the
instrument for two additional days to exhibit it to a potential buyer of similar items. On Tuesday
night, an accidental fire originating from a neighboring shop spreads to Priyanshu’s premises and
completely destroys the instrument. Priyanshu argues that he is not liable because the fire was an
external event not caused by his negligence, and he had taken ordinary prudent care of the
instrument while it was stored.
Assertion (A): Priyanshu becomes strictly liable for the monetary destruction of the musical

XV.	Nuisance is a civil wrong based on unlawful interference with a person’s use or enjoyment of land,
property, or a right connected with property. A person may use his own property, but such use
must not unreasonably disturb another person’s legal rights. The interference may arise through
noise, smoke, smell, vibration, obstruction, pollution, dangerous structures, or any activity that
materially affects comfort, health, safety, or property. For nuisance to be actionable, there must be
a wrongful act and substantial damage, loss, or annoyance. Mere sensitivity or ordinary
inconvenience is not enough. The law examines whether the interference is unreasonable in the
circumstances and whether an ordinary person living in that locality would be affected. Therefore,
the character of the locality, duration of interference, seriousness of harm, and reasonableness of
the defendant’s conduct are important factors. Nuisance is mainly of two kinds: public nuisance
and private nuisance. Public nuisance affects the community or a considerable section of the public.
Under Section 270 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, a person commits public nuisance when
an act or illegal omission causes common injury, danger, or annoyance to the public or to persons
using a public right. Blocking a public road, polluting a public water source, or creating danger ina
public place may amount to public nuisance.
An individual can sue for public nuisance only when he suffers special damage beyond what the
general public suffers. The injury must be direct, substantial, and different in degree from the
inconvenience suffered by others. Section 91 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 also permits legal
action for public nuisance in appropriate cases. Private nuisance affects a specific person’s use or

enjoyment of land. It may involve physical injury to property or physical discomfort to the occupier.
In cases of property damage, sensible injury is usually sufficient. In cases of physical discomfort,
the interference must exceed ordinary use and affect the normal comfort of human life. The main
remedies for nuisance are injunction, damages, and abatement. Injunctions may be granted under
the Specific Relief Act, 1963 to restrain continuing or threatened nuisance. Damages compensate
the injured party for loss suffered. Abatement allows the affected person to remove the nuisance,
but only with reasonable notice and reasonable force. The recognised defences include prescription
and statutory authority. Prescription may apply when the nuisance has continued openly,
peacefully, and without interruption for the required legal period. Statutory authority may protect
an act authorised by law, provided reasonable precautions are taken. However, statutory
permission does not justify unnecessary or negligent harm. [Word Count: 423]

content.questionText:
Parul obtains a valid state license to operate a metal-polishing unit next to Princy’s established
coaching centre. To save on initial setup costs, Parul chooses not to install the recommended rubber
vibration-absorbers under her heavy machinery. When the unit functions, frequent vibrations
shake Princy’s classroom boards and a chemical smell enters the windows, causing significant
discomfort to the students and disrupting classes. Princy sues Parul for private nuisance. Parul
argues that her state license provides her with complete statutory authority to operate the unit.
Will Princy’s suit succeed?
options:
Yes, because a state license only governs regulatory compliance and can never be pleaded as a
defense against an action for private nuisance.

Yes, because statutory authority does not shield an authorized activity if the defendant fails to
take reasonable precautions and causes unnecessary harm.

No, because an activity authorized by a valid legal license is protected by law against claims
based on ordinary personal discomfort.

No, because private nuisance requires an actual physical trespass or direct entry of foreign
objects onto the plaintiff's leased premises.
content.explanation: . The passage explains that while statutory authority protects legally authorized acts, it is conditional upon taking "reasonable precautions" and does not justify "unnecessary or negligent harm." By intentionally skipping the installation of recommended vibration-absorbers to save costs, Parul failed to take reasonable precautions, rendering her defense invalid under the passage.

Priyank purchases a residential apartment located directly above a long-established spice
market. For over twenty-five years, a neighbouring shop has ground mild spices for two hours
every afternoon openly and without any complaints. Recently, however, the shop switches to
grinding highly pungent industrial chili peppers without upgrading its ventilation filters.
While other ordinary residents in the building now experience severe coughing fits and
watering eyes due to the intensified fumes, Priyank, who has a rare respiratory sensitivity is
completely bedridden. Priyank sues the shop owner for private nuisance. The owner argues
that the suit must fail because the shop has a prescriptive right to grind spices in an
established market locality. Will Priyank's suit succeed?
options:
Yes, because the defense of prescription cannot protect a fundamental change in an
activity that creates a new, more serious harm affecting ordinary persons in that locality.

Yes, because a plaintiff's rare and severe health vulnerability takes legal precedence over
the historical commercial character of a locality.

No, because the shop has openly and peacefully ground spices for the required legal period,
giving it an absolute prescriptive right over the property's environmental impact.

No, because by voluntarily purchasing an apartment located directly above a pre-existing
spice market, Priyank legally accepted the locality's inherent discomforts.
content.explanation: . The passage states that the seriousness of harm and unreasonableness are critical factors in determining nuisance, and prescription only applies when "the nuisance" (the specific interference) has continued uninterrupted for the legal period.

After heavy rains damage a town, Palak converts the rear portion of her residential house into
a free community kitchen for displaced families. To cook on a large scale, she uses a diesel
generator and an industrial exhaust fan late into the night. The smoke and vibration
repeatedly enter Payal’s adjoining house, disturbing her sleep, worsening her father’s
breathing difficulty, and making ordinary use of the house uncomfortable. Payal files a suit for
nuisance. Palak argues that her activity cannot be considered a nuisance because it is a
temporary, charitable effort necessary for public welfare. Will Palak's defence succeed?
options:
Yes, because the activity serves public welfare and the disturbance arises from the
compassionate and morally necessary use of property.

Yes, because temporary disaster relief work reduces the gravity of the interference and
should be treated differently from an ordinary private commercial activity.

No, because a socially beneficial use of property may still constitute a nuisance if it
unreasonably disturbs another person’s legal rights to enjoy their property.

No, because any charitable activities becomes a public nuisance once smoke and vibration
affect a neighbour's health and safety.

SECTION IV
XVI. The Supreme Court of India has issued notices to the Union Government, the CBSE, and the
NCERT, directing them to file a comprehensive report on their logistical preparedness to
implement a three-language formula in all CBSE schools for Class 9 students from July 1, 2026.
On May 27, while hearing petitioners challenging the CBSE move, the Court declined to grant an
immediate stay on the policy but acknowledged that concerns over “hardship and inconvenience”
warranted review. The Court will hear arguments on July 15 and 16. The casual manner in which
the government is using the CBSE to enforce its contentious language policy once again shows
complete disregard for students, teachers, and parents. On May 15, the CBSE had issued a circular
mandating the study of three languages for Class 9 students from July 1, citing alignment with the
NEP 2020 and the National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2023. At least two of the
three must be native Indian languages. Foreign languages such as French or German could only be
taken as a third language if the first two were Indian, or alternatively as an optional fourth
subject. In a meagre effort to camouflage the hardship unleashed on the students, the CBSE
exempted the third language from the Class 10 Board examination, which would instead be
assessed through school-based internal evaluations, though the marks would still appear on the
final certificate.
Barely weeks earlier, the CBSE had stated that the third-language requirement would be deferred
until the 2029-30 academic year. The abrupt turnabout can only be explained as a political
decision. The move is being challenged in the Court on multiple grounds, including constitutional
ones. The petitioners argue that language is a matter of personal choice and cannot be imposed by
the state. It is also being pointed out that the NEP 2020, in whose name the mandate is being
enforced, promises flexibility and guarantees that no language shall be imposed on any student or
State. The petitioners also argue that the CBSE, as an executive body, lacks the authority to
impose such a sweeping educational mandate without backing from parliamentary legislation,
regardless of what the NEP says, being an executive policy intent and not a statute. Parents and
teachers are alarmed about the added pressure on students just before their Board examinations.
School administrators have flagged a shortage of trained language teachers and the unavailability
of appropriate textbooks. Turning school education into a cultural battleground is not helping
India’s ambition to become a global reservoir of advanced human resources. The Centre should
course-correct before the Court takes up the case again. [Word Count: 433]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from:
https:/ /www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial /language-decorum-on-the-three-language-formula-
in-cbse-schools/article71044771.ece

SECTION IV
XVI. The Supreme Court of India has issued notices to the Union Government, the CBSE, and the
NCERT, directing them to file a comprehensive report on their logistical preparedness to
implement a three-language formula in all CBSE schools for Class 9 students from July 1, 2026.
On May 27, while hearing petitioners challenging the CBSE move, the Court declined to grant an
immediate stay on the policy but acknowledged that concerns over “hardship and inconvenience”
warranted review. The Court will hear arguments on July 15 and 16. The casual manner in which
the government is using the CBSE to enforce its contentious language policy once again shows
complete disregard for students, teachers, and parents. On May 15, the CBSE had issued a circular
mandating the study of three languages for Class 9 students from July 1, citing alignment with the
NEP 2020 and the National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2023. At least two of the
three must be native Indian languages. Foreign languages such as French or German could only be
taken as a third language if the first two were Indian, or alternatively as an optional fourth
subject. In a meagre effort to camouflage the hardship unleashed on the students, the CBSE
exempted the third language from the Class 10 Board examination, which would instead be
assessed through school-based internal evaluations, though the marks would still appear on the
final certificate.
Barely weeks earlier, the CBSE had stated that the third-language requirement would be deferred
until the 2029-30 academic year. The abrupt turnabout can only be explained as a political
decision. The move is being challenged in the Court on multiple grounds, including constitutional
ones. The petitioners argue that language is a matter of personal choice and cannot be imposed by
the state. It is also being pointed out that the NEP 2020, in whose name the mandate is being
enforced, promises flexibility and guarantees that no language shall be imposed on any student or
State. The petitioners also argue that the CBSE, as an executive body, lacks the authority to
impose such a sweeping educational mandate without backing from parliamentary legislation,
regardless of what the NEP says, being an executive policy intent and not a statute. Parents and
teachers are alarmed about the added pressure on students just before their Board examinations.
School administrators have flagged a shortage of trained language teachers and the unavailability
of appropriate textbooks. Turning school education into a cultural battleground is not helping
India’s ambition to become a global reservoir of advanced human resources. The Centre should
course-correct before the Court takes up the case again. [Word Count: 433]

content.passageText:
XVII. It’s true that when people strongly desire something, such as a new shirt, they might feel like they
‘need’ it — but they don’t need it in the same way that they need water or food. Their survival isn’t
at stake. Desire (as opposed to need) is an intellectual appetite for things that you perceive to be
good, but that you have no physical, instinctual basis for wanting — and that’s true whether those
things are actually good or not.
Your intellectual appetites might include knowing the answer to a mathematics problem; the
satisfaction of receiving a text from someone you have a crush on; or getting a coveted job offer.
These things won’t necessarily cause physical pleasure. They might spill over into physical
enjoyment, but they are not dependent on it. Rather, the pleasure is primarily intellectual. The
18th-century philosopher and theologian Thomas Aquinas wrote that these intellectual appetites
are part of what has traditionally been called the ‘will’. When a person wills something, they strive
toward it. If they come to possess the object of their desire, they will find rest in it — and they are
able to experience joy, so long as they are able to rest in the object of their desire.
But, for most people, such joy is fleeting. There is always something else to strive for — and this
keeps most of us in a constant, sometimes painful, state of never-satisfied striving. And that
striving for something that we do not yet possess is called desire. Desire doesn’t bring us joy
because it is, by definition, always for something we feel we lack. Understanding the mechanism by
which desires take shape, though, can help us avoid living our lives in an endless merry-go-round
of desire.
When it comes to understanding the mystery of desire, one contemporary thinker stands above all
others: the French social theorist René Girard, a historian-turned-polymath who came to the
United States shortly after the Second World War and taught at numerous US universities,
including Johns Hopkins and Stanford. By the time he died in 2015, he had been named to the
Académie Frangaise and was considered one of the greatest minds of the 20th century.
Girard realised one peculiar feature of desire: ‘We would like our desires to come from our deepest
selves, our personal depths,’ he said, ‘but if it did, it would not be desire. Desire is always for
something we feel we lack.’ Girard noted that desire is not, as we often imagine it, something that
we ourselves fully control. It is not something that we can generate or manufacture on our own. It
is largely the product of a social process. [Word Count: 442]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://psyche.co/guides/how-to-know-what-you-
really-want-and-be-free-from-mimetic-desire

XVIII. Does extraterrestrial life exist out in the universe? Have aliens visited us?
It's hard to estimate the chances of life and intelligence arising on any given planet because we
only have one and only one example of life and intelligence arising on a planet. But while this
single data point isn’t as useful as multiple data points, it can still come in handy. Whatever your
estimate of life appearing and evolving to intelligence includes, it must confront the bare-naked
fact that it happened here, once.
And there's even more nuance to our little petri dish called planet Earth. As far as our best fossil
evidence can tell, life arose very early on in the Earth's history, less than 500 million years after

the formation of the planet itself. For all intents and purposes life appeared as soon as conditions
were favorable enough for life to appear (geologically speaking).
On the other hand, intelligence took an extremely long time to appear: four and a half billion years
until humans arose and started asking about their origins. This is so late in the history of the
Earth that it's basically the last chance for intelligence. In just a few hundred million years, our
sun will grow too hot to support liquid water on our planet, erasing all potential for a new
intelligence to arise. www.lawpreptutorial.com
In other words, life appeared quickly, but intelligence didn’t come around until the very last
chance. So, is life in general very common and easy to form, and life appeared early in the Earth's
history because that's exactly what life does? Or is life incredibly rare, and the Earth got
exceptionally lucky? And on the other end, is intelligence a precious thing in the cosmos, explaining
why it took so long for it to show up? Or is intelligence relatively common too, and Earth just
experienced a case of very bad luck over the past four billion years?
To answer these questions, researchers at Columbia University turned to statistical modeling with
a technique called Bayesian inference. This technique doesn't just take a model at face value, it
folds in the facts that we know - the fact that life appeared early and intelligence appeared late.
The researchers had to pick a particular model to describe the chances of life and intelligence
appearing on the planet. And the particular model that they picked assumes that there is a
constant chance in any given chunk of time for life and intelligence to appear. What we don't know
is that constant chance. It could be that once conditions are favorable, life has a 10% chance of
appearing in any given hundred million years. Or 90%. Or 1%. And likewise, for intelligence. [Word
Count: 450]

chances-of-life-appearing-on-earth-

XVIII. Does extraterrestrial life exist out in the universe? Have aliens visited us?
It's hard to estimate the chances of life and intelligence arising on any given planet because we
only have one and only one example of life and intelligence arising on a planet. But while this
single data point isn’t as useful as multiple data points, it can still come in handy. Whatever your
estimate of life appearing and evolving to intelligence includes, it must confront the bare-naked
fact that it happened here, once.
And there's even more nuance to our little petri dish called planet Earth. As far as our best fossil
evidence can tell, life arose very early on in the Earth's history, less than 500 million years after

the formation of the planet itself. For all intents and purposes life appeared as soon as conditions
were favorable enough for life to appear (geologically speaking).
On the other hand, intelligence took an extremely long time to appear: four and a half billion years
until humans arose and started asking about their origins. This is so late in the history of the
Earth that it's basically the last chance for intelligence. In just a few hundred million years, our
sun will grow too hot to support liquid water on our planet, erasing all potential for a new
intelligence to arise. www.lawpreptutorial.com
In other words, life appeared quickly, but intelligence didn’t come around until the very last
chance. So, is life in general very common and easy to form, and life appeared early in the Earth's
history because that's exactly what life does? Or is life incredibly rare, and the Earth got
exceptionally lucky? And on the other end, is intelligence a precious thing in the cosmos, explaining
why it took so long for it to show up? Or is intelligence relatively common too, and Earth just
experienced a case of very bad luck over the past four billion years?
To answer these questions, researchers at Columbia University turned to statistical modeling with
a technique called Bayesian inference. This technique doesn't just take a model at face value, it
folds in the facts that we know - the fact that life appeared early and intelligence appeared late.
The researchers had to pick a particular model to describe the chances of life and intelligence
appearing on the planet. And the particular model that they picked assumes that there is a
constant chance in any given chunk of time for life and intelligence to appear. What we don't know
is that constant chance. It could be that once conditions are favorable, life has a 10% chance of
appearing in any given hundred million years. Or 90%. Or 1%. And likewise, for intelligence. [Word
Count: 450]

chances-of-life-appearing-on-earth-

A scientist argues: “Since life appeared very early on Earth, life must commonly arise on suitable
planets across the universe.” Which of the following best identifies the flaw in this reasoning?
options: It assumes intelligence and simple life must appear through the same process.
It draws a broad cosmic conclusion from one possibly unrepresentative case.
It rejects fossil evidence merely because it cannot confirm alien civilizations.
It treats late intelligence as proof that life itself is biologically impossible.
content.explanation: This option identifies the flaw of hasty generalisation. The scientist moves from one known planetary case to a sweeping conclusion about planets across the universe.

XIX. Directions for Questions 103-108: Relationship Note for this puzzle
Use the following standard meanings:
First cousins share the same grandparents.
Second cousins share the same great-grandparents but NOT the same grandparents.
First cousin once removed means a one-generation gap from a first-cousin relationship.
Second cousin once removed means a one-generation gap from a second-cousin relationship.
At the annual Malhotra Family Reunion, eight relatives sat around a circular table, all facing the
centre.
The eight people were Neeraj, Kavya, Rohan, Simran, Isha, Manav, Tara, and Ved.
The family background was as follows:
* Govind and Leela were the common ancestors of the branch gathered here.
+ Their two sons were Prakash and Suresh.
+ Prakash had three children: one daughter, Asha; one son, Bimal; and one daughter, Chitra.
+ Asha had two children: one son, Neeraj, and one daughter, Kavya.

+ Bimal had one son, Rohan.
+ Chitra had two daughters, Simran and Isha.
- Suresh had one daughter, Nandini.
* Nandini had two children: one son, Manav, and one daughter, Tara.
* Manav had one son, Ved.
Thus, Neeraj, Kavya, Rohan, Simran, and Isha belong to the same first-cousin generation. Except
for sibling pairs, they are first cousins of one another.
Manav and Tara are second cousins of Neeraj, Kavya, Rohan, Simran, and Isha.
Ved is second cousin once removed to Neeraj, Kavya, Rohan, Simran, and Isha.
The seating clues are as follows:
+ Rohan sat immediately counterclockwise of Ved.
+ Simran sat immediately clockwise of Ved.
+ Kavya sat immediately clockwise of Simran.
* Rohan sat opposite Manav.
- Isha sat immediately clockwise of Manav.
+ Neeraj sat immediately clockwise of Isha.
* Tara sat immediately clockwise of Neeraj.
+ The sibling pair from Nandini's branch (Manav and Tara) were not seated adjacent to each
other.
After the reunion, the organiser claimed that the seating arrangement had worked well because no
one was seated only with members of their own family branch. Instead, relatives sat next to people
from different branches, encouraging a wider interaction and conversations across the entire family
rather than within small family groups.
A family historian disagreed. She argued that a successful dinner does not prove that the seating
pattern itself caused wider interaction. In her view, the conversation may have depended on
personal interests, age, profession, humour, or people speaking across the table rather than only to
those seated beside them.
The family committee decided to review the seating notes and feedback cards before deciding
whether to repeat the same seating principle next year.

Neeraj — Tara — Rohan — Ved — Kavya — Simran — Manav — Isha
Neeraj — Tara — Ved — Rohan — Simran — Kavya — Manav — Isha
Neeraj — Isha - Manav — Kavya — Simran — Ved — Rohan — Tara
content.explanation: This is correct because it satisfies every directional and opposite-seat clue.

L	There was once a very learned man in the north-country who knew all the languages under the sun,
and who was acquainted with all the mysteries of creation. He had one big book bound in black calf and
clasped with iron, and with iron corners, and chained to a table which was made fast to the floor; and
when he read out of this book, he unlocked it with an iron key, and none but he read from it, for it
contained all the secrets of the spiritual world.

nineteenth century but circulating long before. Even though you probably haven't read it, it may well
seem familiar (that's pretty much the definition of a folktale). And when you read the start of the next
paragraph— "Now the master had a pupil who was but a foolish lad"— it is probably clear already

into read aloud inadvertently from, or otherwise mishandle this magic book, with terrible
consequences.

red- and- black printed pages, there is a clap of thunder. The room darkens. Before him there appears

Beelzebub, whom he had called up to serve him." Asked by this terrifying apparition to set him to a
task, the pupil panics. In a strangely domestic moment, he asks the demon to water a potted geranium.

have drowned all Yorkshire." The master returns in the nick of time, to speak the countercharm that

content.passageText:
I.	What is mind? In short, the mind is nothing but a cluster of thoughts. Thoughts come into the mind,
they are sustained for some time and then are destroyed. We can’t control our mind. We do not know
which thoughts will come. Both good and bad thoughts rise in our mind, and we suffer due to our
thoughts. If the thoughts are bad or ill, we suffer more. We are helpless.
Another nature of our mind is restlessness. Thoughts come into our mind frequently, and this restless
nature of mind is another cause of our suffering.
Vedanta says the world is nothing but an illusion. We are hypnotised by this illusion. This illusion, or
maya, has two powers. One is that it covers the truth, and the other is that it twists the real and shows
it differently. Due to this illusion, we can’t identify the real nature of the world, and we are attracted
towards it. The more we are attached to the world, the more we are disturbed and become restless. The
only way to free ourselves from this situation is detachment. Do not mix with the material world.
How do you detach yourself from the world? Analysis is the main tool on the path of knowledge.
Analyse what is permanent and what is temporary. In the world around you, whatever you see is not
permanent. All will be destroyed in the course of time; therefore, their existence is time limited.
Discard these worldly things through proper analysis.
Another way of anchoring the restless mind is meditation, the way to anchor the mind on one thought,
discarding all other thoughts. Concentrate on any deity you like. By continuously thinking about that
deity, the mind becomes settled.
It is said that the real nature of yourself is always reflected in your mind. However, due to the restless
nature of the mind, the real nature is not revealed. By meditation, we can settle down the mind and
realise our true nature.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-edit-
page/anchoring-the-restless-mind/

Ill.	Mental health services should focus on lifestyle interventions to improve the physical health of the
mentally ill because physical health conditions are responsible for 70% of the deaths of people with
severe mental illness, according to a new Lancet Psychiatry Physical Health Commission report.
The report, ‘Implementing lifestyle interventions in mental health care’, prepared by a group of 30
experts from 19 countries, recommends that rather than just drug-based therapy, physical
interventions to improve the four modifiable pillars of lifestyle — physical activity, nutrition, smoking
cessation and sleep — are key to improving mental health as well as physical health.
This is especially relevant for mental health services in resource-poor settings like ours where we
seldom look beyond medications and counselling services to address mental health issues. The
cardiometabolic risk factors in those with mental illnesses are at least 1.4 to 2 times higher than in
people without mental illnesses. Our research evidence shows that investing in improving these
metabolic risk factors such as diet, physical activity and sleep can bridge the current 13-15 year
reduction in life expectancy in people with mental illnesses.
In 2019, The Lancet Psychiatry Commission established that people with mental health issues face
significant health inequalities, with regard to their physical health. It said that individuals with
mental illness have a higher lifelong risk of obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular diseases, which
reduced their lifespan by up to 20 years. The Commission had then called for systemic changes to
reduce these preventable health disparities. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Many people living with mental health issues face barriers when it comes to being physically active or
following a good diet. Side effects of the psychotropic drugs they are on also makes them more
vulnerable to weight gain and consequential metabolic syndrome, which impacts their mental health
further. Lifestyle interventions addressing these metabolic risk factors are central to their well being
and should thus be included as crucial adjuvant therapies to medication and psychological therapy.
This means that health systems should remodel their mental health services, train healthcare
personnel to implement these interventions and create adequate support systems for those with mental
illnesses to enable these changes.

content.passageText:
IV.	Alex Foster’s sparky debut novel is built around a new technology of travel. Pods launch high into the
sky and connect with one of thousands of “circuit vessels”, all orbiting the world from east to west.
Travellers then descend in another pod, arriving wherever they choose. Spring-loaded pads store the
pod’s kinetic energy when they land, and propel them up again when they launch. It’s so cheap, so
rapid and so ubiquitous that everyone uses it. You can work in London, meet a friend for lunch in New
York and come back to work that afternoon.
The novel’s narrator, Tanner Kelly, has grown up in rural Alaska, a backwater without a pod station.
He is only too glad to escape, getting a glamorous job in London as personal assistant to scientist Victor
Bickle, who works for CWC, the company that runs the network. Bickle’s job is selling CWC’s services
and whitewashing their effects. As the company’s booming chief of communications, Cromwell Grant,
tells Tanner: “every CWC customer demands two things. He demands the products and services we
provide. And he demands a clean conscience with which to consume them.”
The clean conscience is an issue because the pod technology is harming the world, accelerating the
Earth’s rotation. CWC deny that “day contraction” has anything to do with pod transportation, but this
is a lie. This effect is small-scale at first, days becoming a few minutes shorter, but across the course of
the novel we go from days of 23 hours and 45 minutes to days of 22 hours, of 20 hours, of 12 hours, the
Earth spinning more and more rapidly. Foster likens it to ants on a floating log. Since every action has

an equal and opposite reaction, 1,000 ants all running on top of the log in the same direction will spin
the log beneath them. Workdays contract, circadian rhythms are shattered, people take stimulants to
stay awake and then sedatives to get any sleep.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from:
hittps://www.theguardian.com/books/2025/aug/20/circular-motion-by-alex-foster-review-what-if-the-
world-spun-faster-and-faster
content.questionText: Which option best captures the central tension driving the narrative?
options: Tech utopia without real costs.
Convenience masking planetary time costs.
Rural parity through universal access.
Denial rooted in public ignorance.
content.explanation: The passage pairs mass adoption (“everyone uses it”) with externalized harms (shorter days), making the ethical center a bargain of convenience for ecological cost; the tension is precisely the masking of those time costs through PR and denial.

VI.	The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) will be reattempting the launch of the PSLV-C62
mission, which failed in January, around June this year, the Union Minister of Science and Technology
and Space said on Monday. Minister stressed that none of the foreign passengers booked on PSLV-C62
had withdrawn. “The success rate of our launches is still pretty high compared to any other country
around the world. We have been riding high on success, and yes, these failures have come as a
disappointment, but we are working to rectify them and be back in the game,” the minister said. He
said that the back-to-back failures of ISRO’s workhorse rocket, the PSLV, have in no way impacted its
credibility in the global launch market. He said that none of the foreign customers—scheduled to
launch with ISRO in the coming months—has withdrawn or shown any lack of confidence in India as a
launch partner. On 12 January, ISRO launched its PSLV-C62 mission carrying the strategic satellite
Earth Observation Satellite (EOS-N1), along with 15 other Indian and foreign co-passenger payloads.
However, just minutes after launch, the rocket encountered an anomaly and was unable to place the
satellites in their intended orbit.
This was the second failure of the PSLV rocket in a row, which raised serious doubts about its image as
a reliable commercial satellite carrier. The concerns were even more urgent because this was the first
time India had launched a foreign satellite after the space agency had failed a foreign customer. The
minister also said that the two PSLV missions that had failed, PSLV-C61 in May 2025 and PSLV-C62
in January this year, were unrelated. “It wasn’t the same problem. When the first mission failed, there
was a detailed assessment, and the problem was fixed. Both the issues were different,” he said. He also
added that separate internal and external failure-assessment committees have been set up to analyse
what went wrong in each mission.

disappointment, but we are working to rectify them and be back in the game,” the minister said. He
said that the back-to-back failures of ISRO’s workhorse rocket, the PSLV, have in no way impacted its
credibility in the global launch market. He said that none of the foreign customers—scheduled to
launch with ISRO in the coming months—has withdrawn or shown any lack of confidence in India as a
launch partner. On 12 January, ISRO launched its PSLV-C62 mission carrying the strategic satellite
Earth Observation Satellite (EOS-N1), along with 15 other Indian and foreign co-passenger payloads.
However, just minutes after launch, the rocket encountered an anomaly and was unable to place the
satellites in their intended orbit.
This was the second failure of the PSLV rocket in a row, which raised serious doubts about its image as
a reliable commercial satellite carrier. The concerns were even more urgent because this was the first
time India had launched a foreign satellite after the space agency had failed a foreign customer. The
minister also said that the two PSLV missions that had failed, PSLV-C61 in May 2025 and PSLV-C62
in January this year, were unrelated. “It wasn’t the same problem. When the first mission failed, there
was a detailed assessment, and the problem was fixed. Both the issues were different,” he said. He also
added that separate internal and external failure-assessment committees have been set up to analyse
what went wrong in each mission.

geoeconomic relations between the two. However, the deal awaits ratification by the European
Parliament, EU member states, and India before entering into force. Ratification appears likely, given
the strategic incentives on both sides to diversify economic and geopolitical partnerships. But the
process may be protracted and politically contested, GeoQuant, a unit of Fitch Solutions, has said.
Some members of the EU may raise concerns over sensitive sectors and regulatory standards. Domestic
political pressures can also play a role in the ratification of the FTA, as with past EU trade agreements.
Fitch unit said that parliamentary scrutiny could also slow the ratification progress in India,
particularly where stakeholders question the enforceability of FDI provisions or seek further revisions
on carbon-related measures and agricultural market access. The formal signing of the India-EU free
trade agreement will take place after legal scrubbing, Commerce Secretary had said earlier, following
which the deal will move towards ratification on both sides. GeoQuant's risk chart on India's
Investment/Trade Policy continues to fall, supported by the conclusion of a landmark Free Trade
Agreement with the EU.
The trade agreement will be one of the most comprehensive trade pacts either side has signed. This
ends nearly two decades of stop-start talks between the two economies. The India-EU trade pact is
expected to benefit sectors such as machinery, automotive, pharmaceuticals, and financial services,
while granting Indian exports, including textiles, engineering goods, and spices, improved access to the
EU market. It would also foster deeper integration in services, investment flows, and labour mobility.
The commerce minister said that both sides chose to defer or ring-fence politically and economically
sensitive issues to arrive at what he described as a balanced outcome. www.lawpreptutorial.com

India’s role as a messenger of peace and stability in a world that is increasingly fractious. Ms. Murmu
highlighted recent national achievements and touched upon political and cultural themes that are
currently the priorities of the Centre. She noted that the national song, Vande Mataram, was a “Lyrical
national prayer” even as the country celebrates the 150th anniversary of its composition, and also paid
tribute to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, whose 150th birth anniversary was celebrated recently, for his role

well on track, and commended economic reforms such as the GST and the new Labour Codes. She noted
the great strides achieved by the country’s women in fields ranging from agriculture to space, and their
critical role as voters. Farmers, sanitation workers, teachers, scientists, and healthcare professionals
also found special mention in the President’s speech.

X.	In a departure from the past, India has not allocated any funds for the Chabahar port project in its
Union Budget, a move that came against the backdrop of Washington's fresh sanctions on Iran. In the
last few years, India has been making an annual outlay of Rs 100 crore to the mega connectivity project
in the Sistan-Balochistan province in Iran's southern coast. India is a major partner in the development
of the Chabahar port. In September last year, the US imposed crippling economic sanctions on Iran,
but had granted India a six-month exemption from the punitive measures on the Chabahar port
project. Last month, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said New India is
engaged with the US on the issue related to the Chabahar port project. It is learnt that India was
mulling various options relating to the project after the Trump administration threatened a 25 per cent
additional tariff on countries doing business with Tehran. The Chabahar port is being developed by
India and Iran to boost connectivity and trade ties. Both countries are also strongly pitching for making
the Chabahar port an integral part of the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC). The
INSTC is a 7,200-km-long multi-mode transport project for moving freight among India, Iran,
Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, Central Asia and Europe. Chabahar has been positioned as
a cornerstone of India’s outreach to Afghanistan and Central Asia, and has been used in recent years to
ship humanitarian aid, including food grains and medical supplies.

allocation-for-chabahar-port-project-in-union-budget/articleshow/127837843.cms
content.questionText: What is the strategic importance of Chabahar Port for India?
options: It provides India's naval access to the Caribbean Sea
It gives India direct access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, bypassing Pakistan
It is India’s primary port for trade with the United States
It is a major coal-exporting port for India
content.explanation: Chabahar Port is strategically important for India because it provides an alternative trade and transit route to Afghanistan and Central Asia without passing through Pakistan, which has consistently denied India overland access. Located on Iran’s Gulf of Oman coast, Chabahar allows Indian goods to be shipped by sea to Iran and then transported onward via road and rail links to Afghanistan (notably to Zaranj—Delaram) and further into Central Asia.
