content.passageText:
XIV. Ina landmark constitutional development, the Indian Supreme Court, in MK. Ranjitsinh &
Ors. v. Union of India & Ors. (2024), recognized protection from climate change as a
fundamental right under Articles 21 and 14 of the Constitution, linking the right to life and
equality with environmental integrity. Initially concerning the endangered Great Indian
Bustard, the case expanded to address India's broader constitutional obligations to safeguard
human life, health, and equality in the context of climate change. The judgment builds upon
precedents such as Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1994) and M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath
(2000), but establishes a distinct constitutional right against climate degradation, emphasizing
the disproportionate impact on vulnerable populations including the poor, indigenous
communities, and women. The Court highlighted India's statutory framework, ranging from
the Environment Protection Act, 1986 to the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, and
constitutional directives under Articles 48A and 51A(g), underscoring the duty of the State and
citizens to protect the environment. International jurisprudence informed the reasoning,
including India's obligations under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate
Change (UNFCCC) and pronouncements by UN treaty bodies affirming that failure to mitigate
climate harm constitutes a human rights violation. Comparative references include the Dutch
Urgenda case (2015) and Held v. State (Montana, 2023), illustrating global recognition of the
right to a clean, healthful environment as an extension of human rights. The judgment
foregrounds the intersection of climate change and social justice, noting that inadequate access
to clean energy exacerbates gender inequality and health risks, particularly in rural India. By
framing environmental protection as integral to human dignity, the Court reinforces that
sustainable development, climate resilience, and clean air are inseparable from the right to

life. As observed by Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud, and echoed by UN Secretary-General
Anténio Guterres, safeguarding the environment is central to realizing human rights and
justice in the 21st century. This ruling situates India within a global movement recognizing
environmental protection as a fundamental human right, demanding urgent, rights-based
climate action.
Source: Extracted with edits from the case report on M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. v. Union of India &
Ors. (2024) in livelaw.in

The exemption can stand as long as each project individually meets minimum legal

The cumulative climate harm violates the right to life and equality by neglecting

Economic growth takes precedence over fundamental rights under Article 21 when projects

Judicial review cannot extend to legislative policy choices involving economic
considerations and industrial development strategies

The principle may not straightforwardly apply since statutory permissions exist and no
specific climate harm beyond theoretical assertion has been demonstrated by activists.

The claim stands irrespective of statutory compliance, as Article 21's fundamental rights

The exemption granted by the State amounts to waiver of constitutional obligations under

The law is a valid exercise of State power since the passage confirms the State bears

validation.

industries that voluntarily reduce carbon emissions by 30% within five years. However, the

XV. The Supreme Court of India struck down the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI's) banking ban
against cryptocurrencies on March 4, 2020, declaring the directive as disproportionate and not
applicable to any transaction pre or post judgment. A three-judge bench consisting of Justice
Rohinton Fali Nariman, Justice S. Ravindra Bhat, and Justice V. Ramasubramanian quashed
the RBI's April 6, 2018 circular (the "Crypto Circular"), which restricted banks from providing
services to businesses dealing with cryptocurrencies. The Crypto Circular provided that
"Banks shall not deal in Virtual Currencies/Cryptocurrencies ("VCs") or provide services for
facilitating any person or entity in dealing with or settling VCs. Such services include
maintaining accounts, registering, trading, settling, clearing, giving loans against virtual
tokens, accepting them as collateral, opening accounts of exchanges dealing with them and
transfer/receipt of money in accounts relating to purchase/sale of VCs. Banks which already
provide such services shall exit the relationship within three months from the date of this
circular." While imposing the ban, the RBI had stated that VCs raise concerns of consumer
protection, market integrity, and money laundering, among other risks. The Supreme Court
struck down the Crypto Circular on three principal grounds: first, there was no empirical
evidence of any harm caused by VCs or individuals and entities dealing in VCs to the RBI-
regulated entities, including banks, as set out in the Crypto Circular; second, cryptocurrencies
were not currently banned despite several committees proposing regulations and two draft
bills being discussed—the government had not been able to decide on their legality; third, the
ban was not proportionate to the risk sought to be addressed by such prohibition. The

judgment established that regulatory measures must be supported by demonstrable evidence
of harm and must maintain proportionality between the regulatory objective and the means
employed to achieve it.
Source: Internet and Mobile Association of India v. Reserve Bank of India, Writ Petition (Civil)
No. 528 of 2018, Supreme Court of India, March 4, 2020 (commonly known as the RBI
Cryptocurrency Ban case)

In a futuristic Bollywood film Digital Dhoka, the protagonist Aryan, a struggling filmmaker,
decides to finance his project using cryptocurrency and enters into agreements with several
actors, promising payment in Bitcoin. When Aryan approaches his bank in May 2019 to
transfer funds for location bookings, the bank refuses citing the RBI's April 6, 2018 Crypto
Circular. Aryan sues the bank in 2021, arguing that the Crypto Circular had been struck down
by the Supreme Court in 2020 as disproportionate. The bank counters that since the
agreements were entered before the Supreme Court ruling, they cannot be enforced
retrospectively. Is Aryan's claim against the bank sustainable under the Supreme Court's
ruling?
options:
No, because the bank was justified in relying on the 2018 circular which remained valid
until it was quashed

Yes, because the Supreme Court declared the RBI ban disproportionate and not applicable
to any transaction pre or post judgment

No, because cryptocurrency agreements are void in India as they violate public policy and
regulatory framework standards

Yes, but only if Aryan proves that cryptocurrencies were not expressly declared illegal by
Parliament at the relevant time
content.explanation: The passage explicitly states that the Supreme Court declared the directive "not applicable to any transaction pre or post judgment." This retrospective application means that the Crypto Circular's prohibition is deemed never to have had legal force, including for Aryan's 2019 transaction. XV. The Supreme Court of India struck down the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI's) banking ban
against cryptocurrencies on March 4, 2020, declaring the directive as disproportionate and not
applicable to any transaction pre or post judgment. A three-judge bench consisting of Justice
Rohinton Fali Nariman, Justice S. Ravindra Bhat, and Justice V. Ramasubramanian quashed
the RBI's April 6, 2018 circular (the "Crypto Circular"), which restricted banks from providing
services to businesses dealing with cryptocurrencies. The Crypto Circular provided that
"Banks shall not deal in Virtual Currencies/Cryptocurrencies ("VCs") or provide services for
facilitating any person or entity in dealing with or settling VCs. Such services include
maintaining accounts, registering, trading, settling, clearing, giving loans against virtual
tokens, accepting them as collateral, opening accounts of exchanges dealing with them and
transfer/receipt of money in accounts relating to purchase/sale of VCs. Banks which already
provide such services shall exit the relationship within three months from the date of this
circular." While imposing the ban, the RBI had stated that VCs raise concerns of consumer
protection, market integrity, and money laundering, among other risks. The Supreme Court
struck down the Crypto Circular on three principal grounds: first, there was no empirical
evidence of any harm caused by VCs or individuals and entities dealing in VCs to the RBI-
regulated entities, including banks, as set out in the Crypto Circular; second, cryptocurrencies
were not currently banned despite several committees proposing regulations and two draft
bills being discussed—the government had not been able to decide on their legality; third, the
ban was not proportionate to the risk sought to be addressed by such prohibition. The

judgment established that regulatory measures must be supported by demonstrable evidence
of harm and must maintain proportionality between the regulatory objective and the means
employed to achieve it.

XVI. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act),
operationalizing Article 21A of the Constitution, mandates free and compulsory education for
all children aged 6-14 years and was enforced from April 1, 2010. The constitutional journey
toward this right began with Article 45, a non-justiciable Directive Principle directing the
State to provide free education to children up to age 14 within ten years of the Constitution's
commencement. Judicial intervention transformed this aspiration into enforceable law through
Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992), which read the right to education into Article 21,
and Unnikrishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), which held that free education up to age
14 is a fundamental right. The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A,
guaranteeing free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14, amended Article 45 to
provide for early childhood care for children below six years, and added Article 51A(k)
imposing a fundamental duty on parents and guardians to provide educational opportunities.
The RTE Act establishes minimum norms for school infrastructure, teacher qualifications, and
pupil-teacher ratios while prohibiting physical punishment, capitation fees, screening
procedures, and denial of admission. Critically, Section 12(1)(c) requires private unaided
schools to reserve 25% of entry-level seats (Class I or pre-primary where it exists) for children
from economically weaker and disadvantaged groups, with State reimbursement to the extent
of per-child expenditure in government schools. Educational institutions are categorized into:
government schools (fully state-funded), aided private schools (privately managed but
receiving financial aid, obligated to provide free seats proportionate to aid received), unaided
private schools (privately managed without state funding), and minority educational
institutions established and administered by linguistic or religious minorities under Article

80(1). In Society for Unaided Private Schools v. Union of India (2012), the Supreme Court
upheld the RTE Act's applicability to government, aided, and unaided non-minority private
schools while exempting unaided minority institutions. Subsequently, the five-judge
Constitution Bench in Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014) held
that the RTE Act is entirely inapplicable to minority institutions—both aided and unaided—
reasoning that forcing admission of 25% children from outside the minority community would
dilute their character and infringe their Article 30(1) right to administer institutions of their
choice. This exempted minority institutions from all RTE obligations, not merely Section
12(1)(c). Recently, a two-judge Bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and Manmohan
questioned the correctness of Pramati, observing that exempting minority schools may
jeopardize Article 21A rights of children studying therein. The Court emphasized that Article
80(1) minority rights and Article 21A child education rights must be harmoniously interpreted
rather than one trumping the other, and referred the question to a larger Constitution Bench
for reconsideration.
Source: extracted with edits and revision from https: //www.scobserver.in/journal/should-
certain-provisions-of-the-rte-act-apply-to-minority-educational-institutions.

jeopardize Article 21A rights of children studying therein. The Court emphasized that Article

rather than one trumping the other, and referred the question to a larger Constitution Bench
for reconsideration.

SECTION IV
XVII. One of the less celebrated successes of India’s counter-terrorism operations has been the effort
of security agencies to isolate, localise and de-politicise counter-radicalisation campaigns so
that no religious or ethnic community feels unduly targeted. In fact, such campaigns have

prospective deviant away from the path of radicalisation.

topic that has been a subject of heated political debate world- wide. While Western states have

reportedly shown better results in Southeast Asian countries. Given the mixed results, Indian
central and state governments have been largely reluctant to introduce Western-style
individual - centric de- radicalisation programmes.
It is also heartening to note that Indian counter-terrorism policy is well in the know about the
abuse of social media platforms and instant messaging applications for "communication,
funding and guiding terror attacks" and has on its radar the threats posed by “encryption,
dark web, crypto, wallets etc". 'The paper makes special mention of Pakistan-based cross-
border threats posed by drones and expresses concerns over CBRNED (chemical, biological,
radiological, nuclear, explosive, digital) threats. Highlighting these concerns in a policy paper
is often indicative of steps taken to counter the threats without making them public.
'The policy document stresses that "India adheres to the 'Rule of Law, where laws are just,
applied evenly and protect fundamental rights". After naming an exclusive list of counter-
terrorism legislation, it points out that "multiple levels of legal redressal are available to any
accused through an elaborate infrastructure of the justice system from the districts, through
states, right up to the higher judiciary at the central level. The due process of law gives wide
scope to the Supreme Court for protection of the rights of citizens.

we may well question the need to publish the document now. One can only speculate that as
part of India’s ongoing Operation Sindoor, the government now seeks to launch a major public
relations campaign to clear any misapprehensions regarding its commitment towards
combating terrorism. In any case, India’s first counter- terrorism policy document is a welcome
step in the right direction and, like the title of its concluding section, it duly charts a visionary
"Way Forward'.

content.passageText:
XVIII. When the ICC was created, it was hailed as a "victims' court". Survivors of mass atrocities
would not only testify, but also have the right to be heard at all stages of proceedings. Through
their legal representatives, victims could comment on decisions to open investigations, admit
or reject cases, shape the scope of charges, submit observations to judges, question witnesses,
and participate in determining reparations—provided such participation did not prejudice the
rights of the accused or the fairness of the trial.
To facilitate this engagement, the ICC established the Victims Participation and Reparations
Section (VPRS), a dedicated unit to assist victims in navigating complex legal procedures.
Together, these innovations were intended to give the Court a restorative dimension, reflecting
a growing global consensus that justice must encompass participation, recognition, and repair.
Over the past two decades, thousands of victims have been registered as participants before
the ICC, with thousands more seeking recognition. Currently, more than 18,000 victims are
participating directly or indirectly in proceedings across 34 cases. In its 24 years of operation,
the ICC has facilitated victim participation and reparations through the Trust Fund,
demonstrating the scheme's enduring relevance.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Victims' participation under Article 68(3) and reparations under Article 75 provide procedural
standing unparalleled in international criminal justice. Yet, significant challenges persist.
Procedural complexities, inconsistent jurisprudence, limited financial resources, and political
constraints often undermine the effectiveness of these mechanisms. Ensuring meaningful
participation— rather than symbolic inclusion—remains a persistent challenge, particularly
given the scale and diversity of victims in mass atrocity situations.

The tension between victims' rights and the accused's right to a fair and expeditious trial
further complicates the Court's work. The ICC's annual budget for 2026 stands at
approximately €196.8 million, much of which is absorbed by trial and operational costs. Of the
34 cases admitted so far, the Court has delivered 13 convictions and four acquittals—figures
that highlight the slow pace of international criminal trials.
Structural limitations also persist. The ICC depends heavily on State cooperation for arrests
and enforcement, yet many countries—including India—are not parties to the Rome Statute.
Among the permanent members of the UN Security Council, only France and the United
Kingdom are members of the ICC.
Despite these constraints, the Court has restored a measure of confidence among victims that
international justice is possible and that impunity is not guaranteed—even for presidents and
prime ministers. The ICC remains one of the few permanent institutions striving to uphold an
international rule of law while giving voice to victims long silenced by mass violence. In doing
so, it ensures that the world not only hears those voices—but responds to them.
Source: https://indialegallive.com/column-news/international-criminal-court-victims-rights

XIX. Germany is facing a strange reckoning. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is asking Germans
to work more if the country is to maintain its standards of living. The call for more work has
been interpreted by many as Merz calling Germans lazy — a stark contrast from Germany's
image of efficiency and industriousness.
In a recent speech, Merz laid out the factors holding back the German economy. He talked
about reducing the bureaucracy, cutting down energy prices, and reducing the tax burden,
among others. But what caught everyone's attention was his call to reduce labour costs — by
working more. He said: "Overall, the work performance of our economy is not high enough...
With work-life balance and a four-day week, the prosperity of our country, which we have
today, cannot be maintained in the future, and therefore we have to work more!"
So, have Germans become lazy?
In 2026, Germany is the world's third-largest economy with an estimated annual GDP of $5.33
trillion. But its position is misleading, because it is way behind the leaders: The US has an
annual GDP of almost $82 trillion and China almost $21 trillion. Even India (with a GDP of
$4.5 trillion) is fast catching up, though it is much poorer in per capita terms.
There are many reasons why Germany has lagged far behind the US and was overtaken by
China. One reason is its population, which has largely been stagnant over the past 25 years,
and even this stagnant level of population is propped up by immigrants because left to itself,
Germany has been experiencing a negative population growth (death rate being higher than
birth rate).
But more specifically, Merz's contention — that Germans have been putting in fewer hours —
is true. The chart shows how, as Germany became more and more prosperous (rising GDP per
capita), the annual working hours per worker have dropped quite sharply. Contrast this with
what is happening in China (with its size of population), and one sees how China sped past
Germany in overall size of economy.
To be fair, if an average German earns far more in real wages than workers in most other
countries, it does not make sense to work more. But Germany also created laws that hold back
workers from putting in more hours — or at least do not incentivise it. Merz aims to rectify the

incentive structure. For instance, he mentioned lifting the "pre-employment ban", which
legally prohibited people from working longer in their companies beyond the standard working
time limit.
Source: https://indianexpress.com/article/explained /explained-economics/germany-friedrich-
merz-economy-incentives-10530726/

XIX. Germany is facing a strange reckoning. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is asking Germans
to work more if the country is to maintain its standards of living. The call for more work has
been interpreted by many as Merz calling Germans lazy — a stark contrast from Germany's
image of efficiency and industriousness.
In a recent speech, Merz laid out the factors holding back the German economy. He talked
about reducing the bureaucracy, cutting down energy prices, and reducing the tax burden,
among others. But what caught everyone's attention was his call to reduce labour costs — by
working more. He said: "Overall, the work performance of our economy is not high enough...
With work-life balance and a four-day week, the prosperity of our country, which we have
today, cannot be maintained in the future, and therefore we have to work more!"
So, have Germans become lazy?
In 2026, Germany is the world's third-largest economy with an estimated annual GDP of $5.33
trillion. But its position is misleading, because it is way behind the leaders: The US has an
annual GDP of almost $82 trillion and China almost $21 trillion. Even India (with a GDP of
$4.5 trillion) is fast catching up, though it is much poorer in per capita terms.
There are many reasons why Germany has lagged far behind the US and was overtaken by
China. One reason is its population, which has largely been stagnant over the past 25 years,
and even this stagnant level of population is propped up by immigrants because left to itself,
Germany has been experiencing a negative population growth (death rate being higher than
birth rate).
But more specifically, Merz's contention — that Germans have been putting in fewer hours —
is true. The chart shows how, as Germany became more and more prosperous (rising GDP per
capita), the annual working hours per worker have dropped quite sharply. Contrast this with
what is happening in China (with its size of population), and one sees how China sped past
Germany in overall size of economy.
To be fair, if an average German earns far more in real wages than workers in most other
countries, it does not make sense to work more. But Germany also created laws that hold back
workers from putting in more hours — or at least do not incentivise it. Merz aims to rectify the

incentive structure. For instance, he mentioned lifting the "pre-employment ban", which
legally prohibited people from working longer in their companies beyond the standard working
time limit.

merz-economy-incentives-10530726/
